title: Steel Front Bumper for the Tacoma
tools_required: wire harness tools for fog light transfer

citations.title: CBI Offroad Tacoma Bumper Product Page
Expedition One Tacoma Products

summary: The factory Tacoma bumper is plastic-capped stamped steel with poor approach geometry and no winch mount — an aftermarket steel bumper is a foundational upgrade for any serious trail or overland build.
description:
The stock Tacoma front bumper sits low and has a deep chin that reduces approach angle. On moderate trail terrain, the factory lower valance contacts obstacles before the tires do. Aftermarket steel bumpers solve this in two ways: they mount higher relative to the frame and use a tighter, more vertical face that eliminates the low-hanging chin entirely. The improvement in approach angle is typically 5°–8°, which matters on technical rocky terrain.

The Tacoma's OEM bumper has no provision for a winch. To add a winch to a stock Tacoma, you need either a full replacement bumper with an integrated winch plate or a dedicated winch mounting plate (which compromises approach angle and adds weight without structural improvement). The steel bumper is the correct solution — it mounts a 10,000 lb winch directly to the frame through the bumper structure.

On 3rd gen Tacomas (2016–2023), parking sensors are mounted in the front bumper. Most quality aftermarket bumpers include provisions for the OEM sensor mounts — CBI, Expedition One, and Fab Four all offer sensor-compatible drilling templates. Confirm sensor compatibility before ordering and verify whether you need the sensor relocation bracket included or sold separately. The 2nd gen (2005–2015) is simpler — no front parking sensors to worry about.

Stubby vs full-width matters for approach angle and trail clearance. Full-width bumpers are better for parking and low-speed brushing through vegetation. Stubby bumpers improve approach angle further (especially important for rock crawling) but sacrifice the wing protection on the outer fenders. Most overland-focused builds choose full-width; rock-focused builds often prefer stubby or mid-width designs.
steps: Confirm parking sensor compatibility for your year and trim level before ordering
Disconnect battery negative terminal before starting any bumper work involving electrical
Remove OEM bumper: typically 6–8 bolts along the top edge and lower mounting brackets
Transfer fog lights if applicable — most OEM fog light plugs reach aftermarket bumper fog cutouts without extension
Transfer parking sensors if applicable — remove from OEM bumper, install in new bumper per manufacturer drilling template
Transfer any OEM tow hook if desired (most aftermarket bumpers include integrated recovery tabs)
Test-fit new bumper before connecting any wiring — confirm frame mounting alignment
Bolt bumper to frame using supplied hardware; torque to spec (typically 60–80 ft-lb)
Reconnect fog lights and parking sensors; verify function before closing up
Reconnect battery and test all front lights and sensors
If installing a winch: mount winch to winch plate before installing bumper assembly — easier to torque winch bolts with the bumper on a workbench
pros: Substantially improved approach angle over factory — 5°–8° gain typical
Integrated winch plate allows proper 10,000+ lb winch mount without compromises
DOM or plate steel construction survives impacts that would crack or fold the factory bumper
Fog light and parking sensor provisions on most quality bumpers make the swap clean
Recovery tabs (usually two D-ring mounts) are rated and load-tested, unlike factory tow hooks on some Tacoma years
cons: Adds 60–120 lbs of steel to the front of the truck — increases nose weight and can affect steering feel
Full-width bumpers reduce effective approach angle vs stubby designs
3rd gen parking sensor transfer adds complexity — budget extra time and confirm sensor compatibility
Powder coat finish will chip on trail use — touch up with rattle-can primer to prevent rust
Labor-intensive to install solo; a second person makes alignment and bolt access much easier
High-end options (Fab Four, Expedition One) approach $1,400 — verify what's included vs optional

title: Rear Bumper and Trailer Hitch Integration for the Tacoma

parts.name: Addictive Desert Designs Tacoma Rear Bumper

citations.title: CBI Offroad Tacoma Rear Bumper Product Page

summary: A steel rear bumper on the Tacoma improves departure angle, adds proper recovery tow points, and opens the door for an integrated swing-out tire carrier — but 2nd gen owners need to check bed clearance before choosing a swing-out design.
description:
The factory Tacoma rear bumper is a chrome-tipped stamped steel unit with a receiver hitch. It hangs low and offers poor departure angle — the lower edge will drag on steep exit angles before the rear tires lose traction. Aftermarket steel bumpers ride higher on the frame and trim the lower profile to recover 3°–5° of departure angle. That's a noticeable difference when climbing out of a wash or exiting a steep trail.

Recovery point quality is the other motivator. The OEM receiver hitch is rated for towing but the tow ball mount is not an appropriate recovery point. Aftermarket rear bumpers include two proper D-ring tabs rated to the bumper's full load capacity, typically tested to 20,000+ lbs. That's the correct anchor for a kinetic rope recovery from the rear.

On 2nd gen Tacomas (2005–2015), the bed overhang creates interference with some swing-out spare tire carrier designs. The bed narrows slightly toward the rear and the tailgate mechanism is close to the frame. Some swing-out designs swing past the bed edge cleanly; others contact the bed flare at full swing. Check the specific swing arc measurement from the manufacturer and compare to your bed width before ordering a swing-out carrier for a 2nd gen. Most 3rd gen Tacomas (2016–2023) have sufficient clearance for standard swing-out carriers without modification.

Backup camera retention is typically straightforward — most quality bumpers include a camera mount that accepts the OEM camera housing. Confirm before ordering.
steps: Measure current bed width and swing-out arc if planning a spare tire carrier
Disconnect battery negative before any electrical work
Remove OEM rear bumper: typically 4–6 bolts along the bottom and side brackets
Remove OEM trailer wiring plug from bumper (transfer to new bumper or extend harness)
Remove backup camera from OEM bumper if applicable; install in new bumper camera mount
Test-fit new bumper dry before attaching any wiring
Bolt bumper to frame using supplied hardware; torque to spec
Reconnect trailer wiring and backup camera; test all functions
If adding swing-out tire carrier: mount carrier hardware to bumper before installing on truck; load carrier with spare tire and verify swing clearance at full open
Reconnect battery and verify all lights and camera
pros: 3°–5° departure angle improvement — measurable on steep exit terrain
Proper load-rated D-ring recovery tabs for rear recovery
Receiver hitch retained or upgraded on most designs — maintains towing capability
Backup camera provisions on most quality designs
Swing-out tire carrier option frees bed space from a bed-mounted spare
cons: 2nd gen Tacoma bed interference with swing-out carriers — must verify clearance before ordering
Adds 40–80 lbs of steel to the rear — affects payload and departure feel slightly
Backup camera relocation can change camera angle slightly; may need angle adjustment
Swing-out tire carriers carrying a mounted 33"+ spare add substantial cantilevered weight — torque spec on carrier pivot is critical
Cost of bumper + swing-out carrier combination typically runs $1,200–$1,800

title: Skid Plate Kit for the Tacoma — Engine, Transfer Case, and Fuel Tank

parts.name: CBI Offroad Tacoma Full Skid Plate Kit (2005-2023)
Prinsu Design Studio Tacoma Skid Plate Kit
DRT Offroad Tacoma Full Skid System

citations.title: CBI Offroad Tacoma Skid Plate Product Page
ASFIR 4x4 Tacoma Products

summary: The Tacoma's factory skid plates are thin stamped steel that protects the oil pan and not much else — a full aftermarket skid system covers the transfer case, fuel tank, and rear differential with 3/16" or thicker steel that can take a direct hit from a rock.
description:
The factory Toyota skid plate covers the engine oil pan with roughly 1/8" stamped steel. That's adequate for minor debris and gravel but will deform on a direct rock strike and potentially contact the oil pan itself. Aftermarket full skid kits replace and extend that protection to cover everything under the truck: oil pan, transmission, transfer case, and fuel tank. For a truck that sees regular rocky terrain, this is baseline protection — not a luxury add-on.

What each skid covers matters when evaluating kits. A full-coverage system includes the front crossmember and oil pan skid, a center transmission and transfer case skid (often the largest piece), and a rear fuel tank skid. Some kits add a rear differential skid. CBI Offroad and ASFIR kits cover all four areas. Prinsu's kit is priced lower but covers the oil pan and transfer case — verify fuel tank coverage before ordering if you're doing rocky terrain where the rear tank is exposed.

Material choice is steel vs aluminum. Steel (3/16" to 1/4") is heavier but more impact-resistant — it dents but doesn't crack. Aluminum (1/4" to 3/8") is lighter and resists corrosion better, but a sharp rock strike at speed can crack aluminum skids in a way steel won't. For dedicated trail use with rock impacts, steel is the more reliable choice. For overland use where the primary concern is high-centering on rocks, aluminum is a reasonable compromise at lower weight.

Front crossmember gussets are a detail worth checking. The Tacoma's front crossmember is a known weak point under heavy off-road use — it can crack at the welds. Some skid kits include reinforcing gussets that tie into the crossmember mounting. CBI and ASFIR kits include this feature; Prinsu's does not. If you're doing serious trail work, the crossmember gusset is worth paying for.
steps: Lift and support vehicle on jack stands at the frame rails; provide clearance to work under the truck
Remove OEM factory skid plate(s) — typically 3–4 bolts per piece
Clean mounting surfaces of rust or debris
Test-fit each new skid section dry before drilling any new holes
Install front crossmember gussets first if included — these bolt to the existing crossmember hardware
Install front oil pan skid; use existing OEM holes where possible, drill new holes per template if required
Install transmission/transfer case skid — typically the largest and heaviest piece; use a floor jack as a helper to hold it up while starting bolts
Install fuel tank skid, ensuring it clears the tank straps and fuel fill neck
Apply anti-seize to all hardware to prevent galvanic corrosion between steel skid and aluminum frame components
Torque all fasteners to spec; verify no contact with moving drivetrain components by turning driveshafts by hand
Lower vehicle and do a slow test roll to confirm no noise from skid contact
pros: Full kit covers all major underbody components in a single purchase
3/16" steel will take direct rock strikes that would destroy the factory skids
Crossmember gussets (on CBI and ASFIR kits) address a known Tacoma weak point
Skids act as a controlled slide surface on rocks — the truck glides over obstacles instead of snagging
Bolt-on installation with no welding required
cons: Full steel kit adds 60–100 lbs of underbody weight
Aluminum kits are lighter but can crack under sharp rock impact — verify material before ordering
Some kits do not cover the fuel tank or rear differential — read coverage descriptions carefully
Prinsu kit is the most affordable but may require drilling new mounting holes that void OEM frame warranty
Ground clearance is reduced slightly by skid thickness — typically 1/4"–3/8" depending on skid design

title: Rock Sliders and Frame Rails for the Tacoma

parts.name: Total Chaos Fabrication Tacoma Frame Sliders

citations.title: CBI Offroad Tacoma Slider Product Page
Tacoma World Armor and Protection Discussion

summary: Rock sliders are frame-mounted steel tubes that protect the Tacoma's rocker panels and cab floor from side hits — a nerf step or running board is not a substitute, and the difference between the two becomes obvious the first time you side-hill a boulder.
description:
The Tacoma's frame rails run along the outside of the cab, and the rocker panels and cab floor are exposed below the door line. On any trail with rocks, ledges, or side-hill obstacles, one mis-step will dent the rocker or crease the cab floor — repairs that run $500–$2,000 at a body shop. A proper frame-mounted slider takes that hit instead, spreading the load through the frame rather than through the body.

There is an important distinction between rock sliders and nerf steps. Nerf steps like N-Fab's product attach to the body mount bolts and are designed to be stepped on to enter the cab — they are not designed to take a lateral hit from a rock or act as a jack point under load. A frame-mounted slider bolts directly to the frame rail with gussets and plates that transfer force along the frame. Some slider designs also add a tube step for cab entry, which is fine, but the structural connection is what matters. If a product does not specify frame mounting with gusseted plates, treat it as a body step, not a slider.

CBI Offroad's Tacoma sliders are the most common choice — they use 3/16" DOM tubing, bolt to the frame at three points per side, and include a step tube. Total Chaos Fabrication offers a heavier 1/4" wall tube option favored for serious rock crawling where the slider may serve as a pivot point. Metal Tech 4x4 sits between the two in price and wall thickness.

Cab-length vs full-length matters. Cab-length sliders cover from the front door forward to the rear door edge — they protect the primary exposure points. Full-length sliders extend under the rear cab and bed, which matters on access cab or double cab Tacomas where the rear cab area overhangs the frame. For rock crawling where you're using the slider as a fulcrum, cab-length is usually sufficient. For overlanding with loaded beds on off-camber terrain, full-length coverage adds peace of mind.
steps: Clean frame rails with a wire brush — inspect for rust or damage before installing
Place vehicle on jack stands to access the underside
Identify OEM mounting points per slider manufacturer template (some use existing body mount bolts, others drill new frame holes)
Test-fit slider dry before applying any hardware — confirm clearance with tires and rocker panel
Mark drill locations if new holes are required; use center punch for accuracy
Drill frame holes with appropriate bit (typically 9/16" for 1/2" hardware)
Apply anti-seize to all hardware before final install
Install slider with all provided hardware finger-tight to allow positioning
Align slider level with ground and flush against the rocker panel outer edge
Torque all fasteners to spec — most sliders spec 50–75 ft-lb for 1/2" grade 8 hardware
Check clearance between slider and tire at full lock with vehicle at ride height
Touch up any raw steel edges with primer or bed liner to prevent rust
pros: Frame-mounted sliders protect the most vulnerable section of the Tacoma's body from rock damage
Serve as a jack point in the field for a floor jack or Hi-Lift
Most designs add a cab entry step without changing the truck's profile dramatically
DOM tubing construction is more field-repairable than aluminum alternatives
Bolt-on installation — no welding required for most designs
cons: Adds 30–50 lbs of steel to each side — total weight gain typically 60–100 lbs
Nerf steps sold as "steps" are not rock sliders regardless of marketing language — verify frame mounting before purchasing
Some slider designs can reduce ground clearance slightly below the frame rail — measure before ordering
3rd gen Tacoma (2016+) has different frame geometry than 2nd gen; confirm year-specific fitment
Full-length sliders can trap mud and moisture between the slider and frame — inspect and clean annually in wet climates

title: Frame Rust Inspection — What to Look For

citations.title: 1995-2000 Toyota Tacoma Frame Rust — Customer Support Program PDF
Toyota Tacoma Frame Rust: Did Toyota Ever Offer A Recall For This? — Motorverso
Toyota Tacoma Frame Recall — Cherish Your Car

summary: Toyota's own inspection standard considers a 10mm-or-larger hole through the frame disqualifying — but by the time you find a hole that size, the structural rust has been progressing for years. Check seams, overlaps, and the area beside the catalytic converter first.
description:
Tacoma frame rust is the single biggest known issue with these trucks. Toyota ran multiple Customer Support Programs and a class-action settlement covering 1995–2004 and 2005–2010 models because of corrosion-through frames — frames that rusted from the inside out due to insufficient e-coat coverage in seams and overlaps. The 2nd-gen 2011–2015 trucks fared better, and the 3rd-gen (2016+) used a galvanized frame with significantly improved corrosion resistance, but no Tacoma is immune if it lives in a salt belt.

The inspection routine matters more than any single tool. Park on a level surface, use a bright flashlight, and crawl underneath with a small pick or flathead screwdriver. The goal is not to be gentle — you're trying to find the soft spots before they find you.

Start at the passenger-side frame rail beside the catalytic converter. This is the consensus failure spot. Heat cycling from the cat, combined with the rail's location for road salt spray, makes this section rust through first. Tap and probe the frame with the pick. Solid metal rings; rust-thinned metal gives a dull thud and the pick will sink into it. A 10mm-or-larger hole here was Toyota's failure threshold during the CSP — anything visibly perforated puts the frame structurally suspect.

Next, work the frame seams and crossmember welds. Salt and moisture sit in seams where two pieces of stamped steel were spot-welded together. Look for bubbling paint, brown weeping stains running down from welds, and flaking that comes off in sheets rather than dust. Sheet-flaking means the rust has eaten deep enough to delaminate layers — that frame section has lost most of its strength.

The rear shackle hanger area is the third hotspot. Leaf-spring hangers concentrate stress and trap road grime. Rust here can let the shackle pull through the frame under load — a leaf spring detaching at highway speed is a serious safety event.

Don't skip the inside of the frame rails. The rails are hollow boxed structure. Many trucks look fine externally because the rust started inside and worked outward. Tap along the length of each rail; listen for hollow, soft spots. A borescope through the drain holes (if present) will show the inside surface — heavy crust or visible scale means the frame is compromised even if the outside looks clean.

If you find perforation: stop, document it with photos, and contact Toyota with the VIN. CSP coverage has expired on older trucks, but some buybacks have happened case-by-case. For trucks outside coverage, frame replacement runs $8,000–$15,000 in the aftermarket — usually beyond the truck's value. Coating an already-rusted frame doesn't restore strength; it just slows further deterioration.
steps: Park on level ground, set the parking brake, chock the wheels.
Crawl underneath with a bright flashlight and a pick.
Probe the passenger-side rail beside the catalytic converter — Toyota's documented failure spot.
Tap along both frame rails from front to rear, listening for dull sounds.
Inspect every frame seam and weld for bubbling, weeping rust stains, or sheet flaking.
Probe the rear leaf spring hangers and crossmember mounts.
Look inside drain holes with a borescope if available.
Photograph any perforation with a ruler for scale, note the VIN, and contact Toyota.
pros: Catches problems while they're still treatable
Costs nothing but time
Required before any major suspension or armor install on a high-mileage truck
cons: A solid-looking frame may still be rusted internally
Coating won't restore lost structural metal
Frame replacement is rarely cost-effective on older trucks
CSP coverage has expired on most 1st and 2nd gen trucks

title: Front Brake Pads and Rotors

parts.name: Toyota OEM front brake pads (2016+ 3rd gen)
Toyota OEM front brake pads (2005-2015 2nd gen)
Powerstop Z36 Truck and Tow pads

citations.title: 3rd Gen Tacoma Front Brake Pad and Rotor DIY Guide
Tacoma Front Brake Caliper Torque Specs

summary: Tacoma front pads run 40,000–55,000 miles in stock driving; with a 17mm and 14mm socket the job is under 2 hours and costs $110 for pads-only or $310 with OEM rotors. Caliper bracket bolts torque to 90 ft-lb.
description:
The Tacoma front brake setup hasn't changed much across 2nd gen (2005–2015) and 3rd gen (2016–2023). Single-piston floating calipers, vented rotors, and the same general tool set as the 4Runner — though the caliper bracket bolts on the Tacoma take a 17mm socket where the 4Runner takes 19mm. Worth verifying before you start the job; nothing kills momentum like discovering you need a different socket while the wheel is off.

Pad replacement intervals depend on load and how you drive. A stock-tire Tacoma daily-driven in Phoenix will get close to 60,000 miles before pads hit 3mm. The same truck running 33s, a front bumper, and a winch will eat the same pads in 30,000 — front-end weight gain matters. If you've lifted the truck and added armor, expect to step up to a heavier-duty pad compound.

Pad recommendations follow the same pattern as the 4Runner. OEM Toyota for stock-feel quiet operation. Akebono ProACT for a low-dust ceramic that doesn't change pedal feel. Powerstop Z36 "Truck and Tow" or EBC Yellowstuff for built rigs and tow loads — both handle sustained heat better and bite harder at the cost of higher initial dust. Skip the no-name pads at chain stores; they'll squeal and gouge rotors within 5,000 miles.

Rotor wear pattern on the Tacoma is interesting. The front rotors warp more often than they wear, especially on trucks that see creek crossings or river runs — water on a glowing-hot rotor sets it spinning slightly out-of-round forever. Toyota's minimum thickness spec is stamped on the rotor edge. Replace when at or below that figure, or when pulsing through the pedal won't resurface out with a brake-in cycle.

The procedure is conventional. The only Tacoma-specific tip: before pulling the caliper, open the brake fluid reservoir cap. Compressing the piston pushes fluid backward, and if the reservoir is full and the cap sealed, that pressure spike can damage ABS valves on the 3rd gen. Open cap, lay a rag over the master cylinder, compress slowly.
steps: Crack lug nuts, lift, support on stands at the frame, remove wheels.
Open brake fluid reservoir cap on the master cylinder. Drape a rag over it.
Remove the two 14mm caliper slider bolts on the back of the caliper. Slide the caliper off the bracket and hang with a coat hanger or bungee.
Pull old pads out of the bracket. Note clip orientation.
Compress the caliper piston back using a C-clamp and an old pad as a buffer. Go slow.
Remove the two 17mm caliper bracket bolts at the steering knuckle. Lift the bracket off.
Pull the old rotor. If it's stuck, two M8x1.25 bolts can be threaded into the puller holes on the rotor face to back it off the hub.
Wire-brush the hub mating surface to bare metal. Any rust crust here causes runout that comes back as pedal pulsing.
Install new rotor (light anti-seize on hub mating surface only — never on the friction surface). Reinstall bracket and torque to 90 ft-lb.
Install new pads with fresh anti-rattle clips. Light brake grease on pad backs and slider pins.
Slide caliper over the pads onto the bracket. Reinstall slider bolts and torque to 25 ft-lb.
Reinstall wheels, torque lugs to 83 ft-lb.
Pump brake pedal 6–8 times until firm before moving the truck. Top off reservoir.
Bed in pads with 8–10 moderate stops from 35 mph, then 2–3 harder stops from 50 mph.
pros: Common 17mm and 14mm sockets, no special tools beyond a torque wrench
Procedure unchanged 2005–2023 except pad part numbers
OEM Toyota pads quiet and consistent for daily driving
Repair manuals from a half-dozen forums document every step
cons: 3rd gen torque values differ from 2nd gen on lug nuts — check by year
Cheap pads will gouge rotors and squeal under 5,000 miles
Skipping the reservoir-cap-off step can damage ABS valves on 3rd gen
Lifted rigs with 33s cut front pad life roughly in half

title: Rear Disc Brake Conversion — When It's Worth It

parts.name: Trail-Gear rear disc brake conversion kit
SOS Performance rear disc conversion kit
All-Pro Off-Road rear disc conversion kit

citations.title: Trail-Gear Rear Disc Brake Kit
SOS Performance Rear Disc Conversion
Pedders Rear Disc Brake Conversion Kit
All-Pro 2005-Current Tacoma Rear Disc Kit

summary: A rear disc conversion is worth it if you run 33"+ tires, tow regularly, or wheel in mud and water; for a mostly-street Tacoma on factory-size tires, the stock drums are fine and the $700–$2,700 is better spent elsewhere.
description:
Toyota kept rear drums on the Tacoma through 2023, while almost every competitor moved to four-wheel discs a decade earlier. The reasoning isn't laziness — drums make a better parking brake, cost less to build, and the rear brakes on a pickup do less than 30% of the stopping work, so the performance penalty is small. For a stock Tacoma driving to and from work on city streets, the drum brakes are not the weak link. The weak link is the front pads.

The conversion gets real value in three scenarios. First, big tires: 33"+ adds rotational mass and the rear drums struggle to keep pace, especially when towing. Second, water and mud: drums fill with water and lose effectiveness for the first 1–3 stops after a creek crossing, which on a trail can mean the difference between stopping and rolling into something. Discs shed water in one or two rotations. Third, heat: long descents loaded down cook drum shoes faster than disc pads because drums don't ventilate. If you've ever felt fade coming down a long grade with a loaded bed, that's the drum's signature failure mode.

Kit costs span a wide range. Trail-Gear at $700 is the entry point — uses LJ80 calipers and a basic parking brake setup. SOS Performance and All-Pro at $1,200–$1,300 use larger calipers and integrated drum-in-hat parking brakes that work better. The full retail-installed cost including labor and a brake bias adjustment runs $2,000–$2,700.

The install is hydraulic-intensive: you're cutting and re-flaring brake lines, swapping the proportioning valve or rebalancing pressures, routing a different parking brake cable, and bleeding the entire system. A blown brake job has obvious consequences, so this is the right project to hand to a competent shop if you're not comfortable cutting and flaring brake lines. Many kits also require a corresponding proportioning valve adjustment because discs need less front bias than drums — get this wrong and the truck stops crooked under hard braking.

Final verdict: for most Tacoma owners on stock tires running street duty, skip it. For heavy overland builds, trail rigs with 33"+ tires, or anyone who routinely tows, it's a worthwhile upgrade that you'll feel every time you stop.
steps: Park on level ground, set parking brake, chock front wheels.
Lift rear, set on jack stands under axle, remove rear wheels.
Disconnect parking brake cable from drum backing plate.
Disconnect rear brake hose from hard line at axle.
Remove drum, drum shoes, wheel cylinders, backing plate.
Mount new caliper bracket per kit instructions.
Install new rotor over hub.
Mount caliper, route flexible brake line.
Cut and flare hard line if kit requires a new fitting orientation.
Route new parking brake cable per kit instructions.
Repeat opposite side.
Verify proportioning valve setting — adjust if kit specifies.
Bleed brakes: right rear, left rear, right front, left front.
Set parking brake adjuster per kit instructions.
Low-speed brake test in an empty lot before highway driving.
Re-torque all caliper and bracket fasteners after 100 miles.
pros: Better fade resistance on long descents
Performs after water crossings without a dry-out period
Lower maintenance over time vs. drums
Pad replacement is faster and simpler than shoe service
cons: $700–$2,700 cost is real money
Hydraulic work requires brake line flaring and full system bleed
Parking brake on disc conversion is often weaker than the stock drum
Mostly cosmetic value on stock-tire street trucks
Brake bias must be adjusted or the truck stops crooked

title: Rear Drum Brake Service — 2nd Gen

parts.name: Toyota OEM Rear Brake Shoe Set
Toyota OEM Rear Brake Shoe Kit (with hardware)

citations.title: Toyota OEM Brake Shoes 04495-04010
Toyota OEM Brake Drum 42431-04061
AdventureTaco — Step by Step Drum Brake Replacement

summary: Tacoma 2nd gen rear drums are reliable for 80,000+ miles but slow to inspect and a pain to service the first time — once you've done it, the procedure is repeatable and the parts are inexpensive.
description:
The 2005–2015 Tacoma kept rear drum brakes across the production run, partly because Toyota was building a truck and drums handle long durations of light braking without cooking pads, and partly because they're cheaper. They work well enough that most owners only replace shoes when they hear scraping or when a brake inspection turns up a contaminated drum from a leaking wheel cylinder.

OEM Toyota shoes are part number 04495-04010, around $55. Toyota also sells a complete shoe kit (04495-35230) that includes the retaining clips and hardware for both sides — at $95 it's worth the upgrade because the hardware on a 100,000-mile truck is usually crusty and worth replacing in one pass. Replacement drums (42431-04061) are about $110 each and only needed if the existing drum is scored past the wear limit or out of round.

Do one side at a time. Leave the opposite side assembled as a reference photo for spring orientation, return spring placement, and adjuster direction. The Tacoma uses a self-adjusting mechanism that engages when you back up and apply the brakes — if the adjuster star wheel is rusted solid, the shoes won't extend as they wear and you'll get a low pedal even with new shoes installed.

Wheel cylinders deserve a look while everything is apart. Pull back the rubber boots; any wetness behind the boots means the seal is going and the cylinder needs replacement before it leaks onto the new shoes.

After install, you'll need to adjust the shoes manually so they're close to the drum, then bed them in with several back-and-stop cycles in an empty lot. Skipping the manual adjustment leaves the pedal soft for the first hundred miles.
steps: Block the front wheels, loosen rear lug nuts, jack the rear axle and put it on stands. Release the parking brake fully.
Remove the wheel. Remove the two Phillips screws holding the drum to the hub (these are often seized — penetrant ahead of time helps).
Pull the drum off. If it's stuck, thread two 8mm bolts into the two threaded holes in the drum face and turn them evenly to push the drum off the hub.
Photograph the shoe assembly before disturbing anything.
Use brake spring pliers to remove the return springs and the hold-down springs and pins.
Remove the adjuster, the parking brake lever from the trailing shoe, and the shoes themselves.
Inspect the wheel cylinder — peel back boots and check for fluid. Replace if wet.
Clean the backing plate with brake cleaner. Lubricate the six shoe contact points on the backing plate with a thin layer of high-temp brake grease.
Transfer the parking brake lever to the new trailing shoe. Install shoes, adjuster, hold-down hardware, and return springs in reverse order.
Turn the adjuster star wheel to spread the shoes until the drum just slides over them with light drag.
Reinstall drum, Phillips screws, and wheel. Torque lugs to 83 ft-lb.
Repeat on the other side.
Pump the brake pedal until it firms up. With the truck in reverse, do 10–15 stops in an empty lot to let the self-adjuster set the shoes.
pros: Inexpensive parts ($55–$95 per axle in shoes)
80,000+ mile lifespan in light use
Drums tolerate long downhill braking better than discs
cons: First-time service is slow and finicky
Self-adjuster fails when corroded, leaving soft pedal
Performance falls off when wet — drums fill with water on river crossings

title: Front CV Axle Replacement

parts.name: GSP new CV axle assembly (2nd/3rd gen)

citations.title: Toyota OEM CV Axle 43430-04071 (2005-2023 Tacoma)
Toyota OEM CV Axle 43430-04020 (1995-2004 Tacoma)
Tacoma World — OEM CV Axle Replacement Part #s thread
YotaShop NCV69142XDP Extreme Angle CV (1st gen)

summary: A clicking sound on tight turns is a torn outer CV boot that's lost grease and chewed the joint; replace the whole shaft, not just the boot, once the joint has been running dry — the boot fails first, but the damage is already done by the time you hear noise.
description:
Tacoma CV axles are the IFS front-half-shafts that connect the front diff to each front hub. Two main generations to know: 1995-2004 (1st gen) uses 43430-04020, 2005-2023 (2nd and 3rd gen) uses 43430-04071. Both are 4WD-specific — RWD-only trucks don't have front CV axles. The outer joint (at the hub) takes the most abuse because of steering angle; the inner joint (at the diff) plunges in and out and rarely fails on a stock truck.

Diagnosis is fast. A click or pop on tight slow turns (parking lot) is a worn outer joint. A vibration at speed under load is a worn inner joint or, more commonly on lifted trucks, an over-angled inner joint without enough plunge room. If the boots are intact and the joints feel tight by hand, it's not the CV axle — look at wheel bearings or lower ball joints next. On lifted Tacomas at 3"+ lift, the front CV operating angle gets steep enough that the inner joint binds at full droop. Aftermarket upper control arms or a diff drop kit pull the inner angle back to a safe range.

Replacement options divide cleanly. OEM Toyota at ~$380 each is the longest-lasting choice — Toyota CVs typically run 200k+ miles. Quality aftermarket reman from SurTrack ($130) or new from GSP ($150) is the budget choice and works fine for a daily driver. If you're running 33s+ on a 3"-lifted truck and you wheel hard, look at the YotaShop NCV69142XDP extreme-angle shaft for 1st-gen trucks — it tolerates more articulation than stock at a price between OEM and budget aftermarket.

Install is straightforward but requires breaking the axle nut and separating the lower ball joint or tie rod. The big axle nut (30mm or 36mm depending on year) is torqued to 174 ft-lbs and may need a breaker bar with a cheater. Don't reuse the axle nut — it's a single-use stake nut. Get a fresh one. Final torque on the nut is critical — too loose and the hub wobbles, too tight and the wheel bearing overheats.
steps: Loosen the lug nuts and the axle hub nut (30mm/36mm) with the wheel on the ground. The nut is staked — chisel the stake out first.
Lift the front, support on stands, remove the wheel.
Remove the brake caliper and rotor. Hang the caliper from a frame member — do not let it hang by the hose.
Separate the lower ball joint or outer tie rod end to swing the knuckle outward. Use a separator tool, not a pickle fork (pickle fork tears boots).
Pull the CV shaft out of the hub by tapping the threaded end with a dead-blow hammer.
Pry the inner joint out of the front differential with a pry bar — there's a circlip that snaps out with firm even pressure.
Compare new shaft to old — same length, same spline counts, boot orientation matching.
Install the new shaft into the diff first (push until the circlip snaps in — confirm by pulling on the shaft).
Guide the outer splines into the hub. Reattach lower ball joint or tie rod. Torque ball joint to 80 ft-lbs, tie rod to 67 ft-lbs.
Reinstall rotor and caliper. Caliper bracket bolts to 90 ft-lbs.
Install a NEW axle nut. Torque to 174 ft-lbs with the wheel on the ground. Stake the nut into the keyway with a punch.
pros: OEM Toyota lasts 200k+ miles
Budget reman is $130 and works fine for daily use
Two-hour job once you've done one
Visible symptom (click on turn) is unambiguous
cons: Axle nut requires a cheater bar to break
Lifted trucks may need UCAs or diff drop to stop killing inner joints
Cheap reman boots fail early — inspect at every oil change
Single-use stake nut means buying a new one each time

title: Rear Locker for the Tacoma — ARB, Auburn, and Spartan Options
tools_required: bearing press or access to press

parts.name: ARB Air Locker for Toyota 8.4" Rear Differential (Tacoma)
Auburn Gear ECTED Electric Locker for Tacoma

citations.title: ARB Air Locker Product Page
Auburn Gear ECTED Product Page

summary: A rear locker transforms the Tacoma's on-trail capability on loose terrain, rocks, and mud — the ARB Air Locker is the highest-performing option, but the Auburn ECTED or Eaton ELocker deliver most of that capability at significantly lower cost.
description:
The Toyota Tacoma uses an 8.4" ring gear rear differential (sometimes noted as the Toyota 8" or R180 in other Toyota documentation). The 2005–2013 2nd gen Tacoma and 2016–2023 3rd gen share the same basic rear axle housing, but the 3rd gen (specifically the 2014+ carrier — which actually carries through to the 3rd gen) uses a slightly revised carrier design. Confirm your model year and axle code (on the axle tag at the differential cover) against the locker manufacturer's fitment chart before ordering.

The ARB Air Locker is the gold standard for air-actuated lockers. When the locker is disengaged, the rear diff behaves like a standard open differential — no on-road handling compromise. When you flip the switch and air pressure engages the locker, both rear wheels are locked together regardless of traction differential. The engagement is reliable, immediate, and there's no ratcheting or clicking behavior on-road when disengaged. The tradeoff is the air system: you need a compressor, air lines routed to the diff, and a solenoid. Most ARB locker installs add a dedicated on-board air compressor (ARB twin or single compressor, $400–$700).

The Auburn ECTED and Eaton ELocker are electrically actuated — the engagement mechanism is electromagnetic rather than pneumatic, so no air system is required. The ECTED engages fully when activated and behaves identically to an open diff when off. For most trail use the behavior is indistinguishable from the ARB in practice. The Spartan Locker is a budget automatic locker (always locked) — it works but creates understeer on paved corners and clicking noise on tight turns on pavement. Reserve the Spartan for a dedicated trail rig or a vehicle rarely driven on pavement.
steps: Verify rear axle ring gear size and carrier application for your specific year and 4WD/2WD configuration
Order locker to match — confirm 4-pinion vs 2-pinion carrier if noted in manufacturer fitment guide
Drain rear differential gear oil
Remove rear axle shafts (8 nuts each side on the backing plate flange)
Remove differential cover; clean gasket surfaces
Remove carrier bearing caps (mark left/right orientation before removal)
Remove carrier assembly from housing — note shim positions
Press out OEM side gears, spider gears, and cross-shaft; install locker internals per manufacturer instructions
For ARB: install air line fitting in differential cover; route air line to bulkhead through axle housing
Reinstall carrier into housing with original shims; set backlash per spec (0.005"–0.008" typical Toyota rear)
Verify bearing preload with dial indicator
Install new differential cover gasket or RTV; torque cover bolts in star pattern
Reinstall axle shafts; torque backing plate nuts to spec
Refill with GL-5 gear oil; add limited slip additive if manufacturer specifies
For ARB: route air line, connect to compressor, test engagement before trail use
For ECTED/ELocker: route and connect wiring harness; test engagement from cab
pros: ARB Air Locker delivers full locker engagement on demand with zero on-road side effects when disengaged
ECTED and ELocker eliminate the need for an air compressor while still providing on/off-road control
Dramatically improves traction on loose rock, mud, and off-camber terrain
Tacoma's 8.4" rear axle is robust and handles locker loads well
Adds real capability that no suspension upgrade can replicate in low-traction situations
cons: ARB Air Locker requires an air compressor, solenoid, and air line routing — adds $400–$700 to total cost
Spartan automatic locker clicks on tight pavement turns and compromises on-road cornering — not for daily drivers
Differential disassembly requires proper tools and bearing press — not a beginner install
Setting backlash and bearing preload incorrectly causes premature ring-and-pinion wear
3rd gen carrier revision requires confirming fitment by year — don't assume 2005–2023 is one part number

title: 3rd Gen Transmission Shudder — Causes and Fix

citations.title: Toyota Tacoma torque converter shudder — TRCG
3rd gen torque converter shudder — Tacoma World
PSA Check Your Trans Fluid Level — Tacoma3G

summary: The shudder you feel between 30 and 50 mph on a 3rd gen Tacoma is the torque converter clutch slipping under flex-lock — start with a fluid level check and a drain-and-fill of Toyota WS, and escalate to torque converter replacement under warranty only if the shudder persists.
description:
The Aisin A750F six-speed automatic in the 3rd gen Tacoma (2016–2023) has a known shudder under light-throttle cruising, typically between 30 and 50 mph in 5th or 6th gear. The cause is torque converter clutch slip — Toyota calls the partial lockup strategy "flex lock," and when the fluid is old, low, or contaminated, the clutch can chatter as it tries to maintain partial engagement. It feels like driving over rumble strips at low speed, or like a manual transmission slipping the clutch.

Three causes show up over and over. First, low fluid: dealers commonly deliver these trucks underfilled because the level check is involved and PDI does not allocate time for it. Owners have found their trucks 1–2 quarts low from the factory. Second, old or degraded WS fluid: Toyota markets WS as "lifetime fluid," but the friction modifiers wear out and the torque converter clutch is the first thing to feel it. Third, an actually damaged torque converter clutch lining, which no amount of fresh fluid will fix.

The fix sequence starts cheap and escalates. Check the fluid level first using the correct procedure: warm the trans to 100–115°F (Techstream or any OBD-II app with Toyota PIDs reads ATF temp), engine running, shifter cycled through every gear, then pull the overflow plug at the bottom of the pan. A trickle means correctly filled. Nothing means low. A gush means overfilled. Add WS through the fill port until you get a trickle out the overflow.

If level is correct and the shudder persists, do a drain-and-fill with fresh Toyota WS (00289-ATFWS). The transmission holds about 11 quarts total but a single drain only removes 3–4 quarts. Three sequential drain-and-fills over a few weeks of driving will exchange most of the fluid without the cost of a power flush. Toyota's official position has been that a power flush is not required, and a series of drain-and-fills is the safer approach.

If the shudder still will not quit, schedule the Toyota TSB repair while the truck is still under powertrain warranty. The TSB process generally includes a fluid exchange, a software reflash that retunes the flex-lock strategy, and torque converter replacement if the clutch lining is damaged. Out of warranty, torque converter replacement at a dealer runs $1,500–$1,800. The aftermarket flat-rate is similar because the transmission has to come out either way.
steps: Verify the symptom: light-throttle shudder at 30–50 mph that goes away when you brush the throttle or shift down. That pattern is flex-lock related.
Check fluid level with the truck warm (100–115°F ATF temp), engine running, on a level surface. Pull the overflow plug — expect a trickle.
If low, top off through the fill port with Toyota WS until a trickle returns at the overflow plug. Replace the gaskets on both plugs.
If level is correct, drain the pan (24mm drain plug), measure the volume drained, and refill the exact same volume of fresh WS through the fill port.
Drive 200–500 miles and reassess. Repeat the drain-and-fill 2 more times over a few weeks if the shudder is improving but not gone.
If the shudder persists after three drain-and-fills, schedule a service visit while under powertrain warranty. Reference the Toyota TSB for transmission shudder.
Replace gaskets on every drain and overflow plug — both are torque-to-yield style copper crush washers and should not be reused.
pros: Many shudders resolve from a level correction alone
Drain-and-fill is $60 in fluid and an hour of work
TSB repair is covered under powertrain warranty (60k miles standard)
Catching it early prevents torque converter damage
cons: Power flush is debated — dealers and forums disagree
Aftermarket fluids labeled "WS compatible" are not always equivalent
Out-of-warranty torque converter replacement runs $1,500–$1,800
Fluid level check requires Toyota PID-capable scanner or Techstream

title: ATF Flush — 5-Speed and 6-Speed Automatics
tools_required: infrared thermometer or OBD scan tool

parts.name: Toyota Genuine WS ATF (1 qt) — 5-speed needs 4 qt per drain, 6-speed needs ~4.2 qt

citations.title: BlauParts — 3rd gen Tacoma ATF change guide
ToyotaNation — Official ATF drain-and-fill how-to
TacomaWorld — Drain/refill thread

summary: Use Toyota WS ATF only. A drain-and-fill swaps about 4 quarts (40% of total), so do it three times spaced a few hundred miles apart to refresh the full system. Final fill level must be set at 95–115°F transmission temp — that part is non-negotiable.
description:
Toyota calls the WS transmission "lifetime fill" and gives no service interval. The trucks that go 250,000 miles got serviced anyway, and the ones that don't go that far usually have an owner who believed the manual. Plan on a drain-and-fill every 60,000 miles to keep the fluid healthy, more often if you tow.

The big constraint: the 5-speed A750F (2005–2015) and the 6-speed AC60F (2016–2023) both have sealed pans with no dipstick. The fluid level is set by an overflow tube — you fill from below, run the truck through the gears at the right fluid temperature, and let the excess drip out the overflow. Get the temperature wrong and you will be 30% over or under, which kills the trans within months. You need an OBD2 scanner that reads ATF temp or a non-contact thermometer pointed at the pan. The target window is 95–115°F (35–46°C).

Total system capacity is about 10 quarts. A pan drain only releases about 4 quarts because the torque converter and cooler lines hold the rest. The accepted way to fully refresh the fluid without a flush machine is three drain-and-fills spaced 300–500 miles apart. Each round dilutes the old fluid, and after three you are at ~80% fresh fluid — comparable to a full machine flush at half the cost.

Use Toyota Genuine WS only, or a real WS-spec equivalent like Aisin AFW+ (Aisin actually builds the transmission for Toyota). Do not use Dexron VI, Mercon V, or universal "multi-vehicle" ATFs — the WS fluid is engineered for low viscosity and the wrong fluid causes shift slippage and overheating within 50 miles.

The fill plug is on the side of the trans housing, accessed with a 24mm socket. The drain plug is on the bottom of the pan, 14mm hex (Allen) bit. There is an inner overflow tube inside the fill plug threads — a 5mm hex (Allen) — that you only touch if you are setting the final level. Open the outer fill plug first to confirm you have a way to refill before you drain.
steps: Drive 10 minutes to warm fluid to operating temp. Park level. Engine off.
Remove the 24mm fill plug on the side of the transmission first. If it is seized, stop — do not drain.
Place pan under transmission. Remove 14mm hex drain plug. Capture fluid (about 4 qt).
Measure what came out. Reinstall drain plug with new gasket, torque to 20 ft-lb.
Using a pump or long-neck funnel, fill through the side plug with the same volume you drained.
With engine running and foot on brake, cycle through all gears (P-R-N-D, hold each 3 seconds), return to Park.
Monitor ATF temp via OBD2 scanner. Wait for 95–115°F window.
With engine still running, remove the inner overflow plug (5mm hex). Fluid will drip out the tube.
When the drip slows to a few drops every 5 seconds, reinstall the inner plug, then the outer 24mm plug. Both get new gaskets.
Drive 300–500 miles, then repeat the full procedure. Repeat once more for the third pass.
pros: Refreshed fluid extends transmission life well past the "lifetime" claim
Catches a leaking pan gasket or weeping cooler line early
$40–$60 in fluid per round vs. $250 dealer service
Builds the skill set for any other Toyota WS transmission
cons: Fluid temp window is strict — wrong level kills the trans
Requires OBD2 scanner or accurate IR thermometer
Sealed pan means no dipstick and no shortcut
Three rounds for a full refresh = real time and fluid cost

title: Cabin Air Filter Replacement

parts.name: Toyota OEM Cabin Air Filter (2006–2023 Tacoma)
Toyota OEM Cabin Air Filter (2024+ Tacoma)

citations.title: Toyota Tacoma Cabin Air Filter 87139-YZZ09
Toyota Tacoma Cabin Air Filter Replacement Guide

summary: 10-minute job behind the glovebox. 2006–2023 Tacomas use part 87139-YZZ09; 2024+ uses 87139-0C010. Swap it every 15,000–30,000 miles depending on how much dust you eat.
description:
The Tacoma cabin air filter sits in a slot behind the glovebox. If you've never changed yours, pull it now and look at it — most Tacomas come into service for the first time at 60,000+ miles with filters that look like a vacuum cleaner bag. A clogged cabin filter cuts HVAC airflow, lets the AC ice up on humid days, and means everything you smell on the trail (dust, smoke, exhaust) is getting concentrated through that filter before hitting your face.

The procedure is the same on every Tacoma from 2005 onward, with minor variations in how the glovebox releases. Open the glovebox fully. On both sides, find the small plastic stop pins or tabs holding the box. Squeeze the sides of the glovebox inward to release these stops — the box will then swing down past its normal stop point. On some years there's also a damper arm on the right side; pop it off its ball joint. The glovebox now hangs free and gives you full access to the filter housing.

The filter housing is the rectangular plastic cover directly behind the glovebox. There's a single tab on the right side — squeeze it and pull the cover toward you. The cover comes off and the old filter slides straight out. Note the airflow arrow on the filter frame — it points down (toward the floor / blower motor). New filters have the same arrow stamped on the frame; install it in the same orientation.

Slide the new filter in, snap the housing cover back, swing the glovebox up and re-engage the stop pins on both sides. Re-attach the damper arm if you popped it off. Test the HVAC fan on high — airflow should noticeably improve on a long-overdue swap.

Phoenix, Arizona owners and anyone running dirt regularly should plan on 15,000-mile intervals. Carbon filters (FRAM Fresh Breeze, K&N HVAC) cost a few dollars more and absorb odors as well as particulates — worth it if you commute behind diesel trucks. Holding a dusty filter up to a shop light tells you everything; if light won't pass through, the filter is done.
steps: Open the glovebox fully and empty its contents.
Squeeze both sides of the glovebox inward to release the side stop pins.
Lower the glovebox past its normal stop point so it hangs free.
(If equipped) Pop the right-side damper arm off its ball joint.
Locate the rectangular filter housing cover behind the glovebox.
Squeeze the tab on the right side and pull the cover toward you.
Slide the old filter out. Note the airflow arrow direction.
Slide the new filter in with the airflow arrow pointing down.
Snap the housing cover back into place.
Re-attach the damper arm and swing the glovebox up. Confirm stop pins re-engage.
Test the HVAC fan on high to confirm airflow.
pros: 10-minute job with no tools required
Restores HVAC airflow and AC performance immediately
Filters odors and smoke when carbon-impregnated versions are used
cons: Most owners forget it exists — it's not on the standard dealer service menu
Aftermarket bargain filters fit loose and let unfiltered air bypass
The glovebox stop pins are plastic and break if forced past their flex range

title: Engine Air Filter Replacement

citations.title: American Toyota Parts — 2005-2023 Tacoma air filter 17801-0C040
Toyota OEM Parts — Tacoma air cleaner element 17801-07020
K&N — Tacoma replacement air filters

summary: The Tacoma engine air filter lives in a black plastic airbox on the passenger side of the engine bay. Pop the four clips, lift the lid, swap the panel filter, snap the lid back down. Five minutes. Toyota wants it changed every 30,000 miles; dirt-road and dusty climates cut that to 15,000–20,000. Match the part number to your engine — 2.7L, 4.0L, and 3.5L all use different filters.
description:
Tacoma airboxes are designed for fast service. There is no cover plate, no intake tube to remove, no clamps. The lid is held by four metal spring clips on each corner of the airbox; pop them open with your fingers and the lid hinges or lifts straight up.

**Three engines, three filters.** The 2.7L 2TR-FE four-cylinder uses Toyota 17801-0C020. The 4.0L 1GR-FE V6 (2005–2015 Tacomas, also used in the 4Runner and FJ Cruiser) uses 17801-0C040. The 3.5L 2GR-FKS V6 (2016–2023 third-gen Tacomas) uses 17801-0P051. They look similar but the seal dimensions differ — the wrong filter will appear to fit but leaks at the corners, letting dust into the MAF sensor and engine. Buy by part number, not by sight.

**Why it matters.** A restricted air filter shifts the engine's fuel trims rich, hurts fuel economy by 1–3 mpg, and accelerates carbon buildup. More important on a Tacoma — the MAF sensor sits just downstream of the filter. Dust that gets past a torn or improperly seated filter coats the MAF wire and gives a permanent rich condition that no amount of cleaning fully fixes. Replace the filter before it tears.

**OEM vs. aftermarket vs. reusable.** Toyota OEM is the gold standard at $20–25. Premium aftermarket (Fram, Wix, Mann) costs the same and works fine. K&N reusable drop-ins (33-5017 for 3rd gen) cost $65 but last the life of the truck — you clean and re-oil them every 50k miles. K&N's filtration is slightly looser than paper. On a daily-driver paved-road Tacoma it doesn't matter; on a dirt-road Phoenix or Moab truck where dust is the enemy, stay with OEM paper and change it more often.

**Inspect, don't guess.** Pull the filter out and hold it up to sunlight. If you can see light through most of the pleats, it's still serviceable. If pleats are gray-black and you can't see light, replace it. Tap it pleats-down on concrete to knock out big debris — this buys you a few thousand more miles between replacements if budget matters.
steps: Open the hood. Find the black plastic airbox on the passenger side, behind the headlight.
Release the four spring clips at the corners of the airbox lid by pulling outward on each. They hinge open.
Lift the airbox lid up and toward the engine. On 3rd gen the lid hinges; on 2nd gen it lifts off entirely.
Lift out the old panel filter. Note its orientation — pleats run side-to-side, sealing edge faces up against the lid gasket.
Wipe the inside of the airbox lower half with a clean rag. Do not blow it out with shop air — that drives dust into the MAF.
Inspect the filter sealing edge of the lid for a clean rubber gasket. Replace lid if torn (rare).
Set the new filter into the lower box, pleats matching the original orientation, sealing edge up.
Close the lid. Latch all four spring clips. Push down on each corner to confirm a flush seal.
Reset the trip odometer or log the mileage. Plan the next change at +30,000 (paved) or +15,000–20,000 (dust).
pros: Five-minute job
$20 part for OEM
Restores fuel economy and protects the MAF sensor
No tools needed on most years
cons: Three different part numbers across engine sizes — verify by VIN before buying
K&N reusable filters filter less aggressively — not the right choice for dusty dirt-road use
Compressed-air "cleaning" of a paper filter damages pleats and reduces filtration
If you see oil residue in the airbox, suspect PCV system, not filter

title: Front Differential Fluid Change

parts.name: Crush washers for drain and fill plugs

citations.title: Blauparts — How to Change Tacoma Front Differential Fluid 2009–2023
Empyre Off-Road — 3rd Gen Tacoma DIY Maintenance Reference
Tacoma World — Differential Drain and Fill Plug Torque

summary: Drain the front differential, refill with 1.5 liters of 75W-85 GL-5 gear oil, torque the fill plug to 29 ft-lbs and the drain plug to 48 ft-lbs — every 30,000 miles for trail-driven Tacomas.
description:
The 2nd-gen (2005–2015) and 3rd-gen (2016–2023) Tacoma share the same front differential service procedure. Capacity is 1.5 liters (1.58 quarts). Buy two quarts to have enough for spillage and a clean refill. Toyota specifies 75W-85 GL-5 gear oil (P/N 08885-81060) — about $22/qt at the dealer. 75W-90 GL-5 from Valvoline, Royal Purple, or Mobil 1 is widely accepted as a drop-in substitute and runs roughly half the price. The Toyota dealer fluid is the safe answer; the aftermarket synthetic 75W-90 is the value answer.

The service interval Toyota publishes is "inspect at 30k, replace as needed" — which for most owners means never. That's fine for a Tacoma that lives on pavement. For any Tacoma that sees dirt roads, washboard, water crossings, or trail use, drain and refill every 30,000 miles. Water intrusion shows up as milky-tan fluid that smells sour. Metal in the fluid means the ring and pinion are wearing — drain it, replace the fluid, and check again in 5,000 miles to see if the trend continues.

The drain and fill plugs are both 10mm hex (Allen) heads, located on the front differential housing. Drain plug is on the bottom; fill plug is on the side. As with every drain-and-fill: break the fill plug loose FIRST. If the fill plug is seized and you've already drained the diff, you can't refill it and the truck is stuck. Once the fill plug is loose, then crack the drain plug.

Crush washers should be replaced with each service. They're $2 from Toyota (P/N 12157-10010) and they're what makes the seal — reusing an old crushed washer is the most common cause of weeping drain plugs. Torque matters here. Drain plug: 48 ft-lbs. Fill plug: 29 ft-lbs. Overtighten and you'll strip the aluminum housing — that's a $1,000 mistake.
steps: Drive the vehicle 10 minutes to warm the fluid. Park on level ground or all four wheels on ramps.
Position a drain pan under the front differential drain plug.
Loosen the fill plug (10mm hex, on the side) FIRST with a 3/8 ratchet and 10mm hex bit. Set the plug and old crush washer aside.
Loosen and remove the drain plug (10mm hex, on the bottom). Let fluid drain fully (5–10 minutes).
Inspect the drained fluid: amber/dark amber is healthy, milky-tan indicates water, glittery indicates metal wear.
Wipe the drain plug magnet (if equipped) clean of metallic fuzz.
Install a new crush washer on the drain plug. Reinstall and torque to 48 ft-lbs.
Use a fluid pump to refill through the fill hole with 75W-85 GL-5. Stop when fluid begins to trickle out the fill hole.
Install a new crush washer on the fill plug. Reinstall and torque to 29 ft-lbs.
Clean any spilled fluid from the housing with brake cleaner.
Take a short drive and recheck for leaks at both plugs.
pros: 30-minute job on level ground with basic tools
$25 in fluid vs. $200+ at a shop
Catches water intrusion and metal wear before they ruin the differential
The drain plug magnet tells you the gear health at a glance
cons: Toyota-spec 75W-85 is roughly $22/qt at the dealer
Stripping the aluminum housing with overtorqued plugs is a $1k mistake
The fill plug is often overlooked and rounds out — break it loose first
Most owners skip this service entirely because Toyota's manual doesn't push it

title: Oil Change — 1GR-FE 4.0L and 2GR-FKS 3.5L

citations.title: Toyota Tacoma owner's manual — oil capacity and viscosity by generation
Tacoma World: filter housing torque 18 ft-lb, drain plug 30 ft-lb

summary: 2nd gen Tacoma (1GR-FE 4.0L) holds 5.5 quarts of 5W-30. 3rd gen (2GR-FKS 3.5L) holds 6.2 quarts of 0W-20 full synthetic. Both use the same cartridge oil filter. Drain plug torque 30 ft-lb, filter housing 18 ft-lb.
description:
The Tacoma's V6 engines share the same oil change procedure across two generations — but viscosity changed when the 3rd gen arrived in 2016 with the 2GR-FKS direct-injected V6. The 2nd gen 4.0L runs 5W-30 conventional or synthetic; the 3rd gen 3.5L requires 0W-20 full synthetic.

**3rd gen oil spec.** The 2GR-FKS uses dual injection (port and direct) and requires 0W-20 to meet the close clearances and ensure fast oil pressure at cold start. Some owners run 5W-30 in hot climates to quiet timing chain noise — Toyota allows this in their hot-climate TSB without voiding warranty. Phoenix, Tucson, and Vegas owners can safely run 5W-30 synthetic in summer.

**Cartridge filter location.** Same setup as the 4Runner: filter housing on the bottom of the engine with a built-in drain valve. The Toyota OEM filter kit (04152-YZZA1) includes both O-rings (large for the cover, small for the drain valve plug) and a small plastic drain tool that threads into the housing bottom to route oil into your pan without spraying.

**Cap socket.** 64mm 14-flute. Steel only — the aluminum versions strip teeth.

**Stock skid plate.** Both gens have a cutout in the front skid that gives access to the filter and drain without dropping the skid. Aftermarket plate-style skids (RCI, Tactica, BAMF) keep this access; some budget skids do not.
steps: Warm engine 2–3 minutes. Shut off.
Lift truck or use ramps. Stock skid plate access port should align with the filter.
Position drain pan under the 14mm drain plug. Remove. Drain 5+ minutes.
Thread the small plastic drain tool into the bottom of the filter housing. Oil drains through it into the pan.
Use 64mm cap socket to remove the housing cover. Lift out old cartridge.
Wipe housing. Replace both O-rings on the cover (large for the cover seal, small for the drain valve plug seat).
Snap new cartridge into cover. Reinstall, torque to 18 ft-lb. Stop there — overtightening strips threads.
Remove the drain tool. Install drain valve plug with its new O-ring. Snug only.
Install drain plug with new crush washer. Torque to 30 ft-lb.
Add 5.5 qt (2nd gen 4.0L) or 6.2 qt (3rd gen 3.5L) of correct oil through valve cover fill.
Start engine. Verify oil pressure light off within 3 seconds. Idle 30 seconds.
Shut off, wait 5 minutes, check dipstick. Top off as needed.
pros: Cartridge filter + drain tool = clean job
100K timing chain on both engines
Stock skid plate has access port
1GR-FE and 2GR-FKS are both proven for 300K+ when maintained
cons: Different viscosity between 2nd and 3rd gen — easy to use wrong oil after a generation change
Drain valve O-ring is the #1 thing forgotten — slow leak after refill
3rd gen carbon buildup on intake valves not fixed by frequent oil changes
5W-30 in a 0W-20 engine works mechanically but trips fuel economy monitors

title: Rear Differential Fluid Change

parts.name: Toyota OEM 75W-85 GL-5 Differential Gear Oil LT (1 quart)

citations.title: BlauParts — How to Change Toyota Tacoma Rear Differential Fluid (2009-2023)
BlauParts — Toyota Tacoma Differential Gear Oil Types Guide
Tacoma Forum — Rear Diff Fluid

summary: The Tacoma rear differential takes 3 to 4 quarts of 75W-85 GL-5 gear oil depending on whether you have the electric locker (TRD Off-Road and Pro) — and unlike older Tacomas, modern A-Trac and e-locker trims do NOT need LSD-specific fluid.
description:
The Tacoma rear axle has gone through a quiet revision that catches owners out. Pre-2009 Tacomas with mechanical limited-slip differentials called for 80W-90 LSD gear oil with friction modifier built in. From 2009 onward, the rear axle specification moved to 75W-85 GL-5 conventional gear oil — Toyota part number 08885-02506, the same fluid used in the front diff. The change reflects the move from mechanical LSDs to the electric locker (e-locker) on TRD trims and A-Trac brake-based traction control on the rest of the lineup. Neither system needs LSD-spec fluid.

If you have a 2nd gen (2005-2015) or 3rd gen (2016-2023) Tacoma in TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro, or any non-LSD trim, use the 75W-85. The only Tacomas that still need LSD fluid are early 2005-2008 trucks specifically optioned with the mechanical LSD — uncommon and identifiable by the LSD badge on the differential cover or in the build sheet. When in doubt, check the door jamb sticker for axle code or call your dealer with the VIN.

Capacity is where Tacomas split. Standard rear axles (no rear locker) hold 2.9 to 3.1 liters (about 3 to 3.3 quarts). E-locker rear axles hold more — 3.8 to 4.0 liters (4 to 4.2 quarts) — because the locker mechanism takes up space differently in the housing. Buy 4 quarts and have a spare in the garage rather than running out mid-fill.

Like every Toyota differential, the right approach is to pump until fluid runs out the fill hole, then stop. Park as level as you can manage; tilt changes apparent fill level.

The plugs are 24mm hex on most 2nd and 3rd gen trucks (some early 2nd gen used a 10mm internal hex). They are torque-spec'd — overtightening crushes the soft aluminum drain plug bosses and creates a leak that's expensive to fix. Spec is 36 ft-lb for fill and drain plugs, and you should use new crush washers each service.

Service interval is 30,000 miles for severe use (tow, off-road, dusty conditions) and 60,000 miles for normal use. If you wheel where water gets above the axle tubes, change immediately after — water destroys ring-and-pinion gears within a few hundred miles.
steps: Park on level ground. Drive a few miles to warm fluid for cleaner drainage.
Slide drain pan under rear diff.
Crack the FILL plug FIRST (24mm hex, upper plug on rear cover). If stuck, stop — do not drain.
Remove drain plug (lower). Let drain fully — 15-20 minutes.
Inspect fluid. Dark brown is normal aging. Milky means water intrusion. Metal chunks mean internal failure — investigate before refilling.
Install new crush gasket on drain plug. Torque to 36 ft-lb.
Pump 75W-85 GL-5 through fill hole until it runs out steady. Standard axles: ~3 quarts. E-locker axles: ~4 quarts.
Install fill plug with new crush gasket. Torque to 36 ft-lb.
Drive a few miles and recheck for leaks.
pros: Same fluid as the front diff on 2009+ trucks — simpler shopping
60,000-mile interval for normal use is realistic; severe service 30,000 is genuinely needed for off-road owners
E-locker does not need LSD fluid — saves the cost of friction-modifier oil
Catches early signs of pinion bearing wear
cons: E-locker trucks need 4 quarts, not 3 — easy to under-buy
24mm hex requires the right bit
Aluminum plug bosses strip if overtightened — must use a torque wrench
2005-2008 LSD trucks still need 80W-90 LSD fluid — easy to mix up if you don't verify trim

title: Spark Plug Replacement — 4.0L V6 and 3.5L V6

citations.title: Toyota Tacoma service info — 100K mi plug interval, 13 ft-lb torque
Denso SK20HR11 OE spec for Toyota 4.0L V6
Tacoma World: rear bank intake plenum removal walkthrough

summary: The 4.0L (1GR-FE) and 3.5L (2GR-FKS) both take six iridium plugs with a 100K mile interval. Rear bank plugs require intake plenum removal — plan 2+ hours your first time. Torque is 13 ft-lb on both engines, gap pre-set at 0.043". Use Denso or NGK iridium; do not regap.
description:
The Tacoma's V6 engines share the same fundamental layout: coil-on-plug with the front three plugs accessible from the top of the engine and the rear three buried under the intake plenum. This is the part most owners aren't ready for — pulling the intake adds an hour, requires removing several vacuum and electrical connectors, and demands attention to the new intake gaskets on reassembly.

**Plug choice.** The 1GR-FE OE plug is Denso SK20HR11 (NGK IFR6T11 is the equivalent). 2GR-FKS uses Denso FK20HBR11 or NGK ILZKR7B11. All are iridium long-life, factory-gapped at 0.043", and last 100,000 miles. Don't regap iridium — the precious metal tip is thin and chips when bent. Don't use copper plugs as a "cheap alternative" on these engines; the coil-on-plug system is tuned for the higher resistance of iridium and copper causes misfires under load.

**Front bank.** Front three plugs are visible after removing the engine cover. Pull each coil's 10mm bolt, disconnect the harness clip, and lift the coil out. Plug socket goes straight down.

**Rear bank.** Rear three sit between the intake plenum and the firewall. You have to remove the plenum to reach them. This means:

- Disconnect throttle body harness and unbolt the throttle body (4 bolts)
- Disconnect EVAP, PCV, and brake booster vacuum lines
- Unbolt the plenum (10mm bolts, sequence matters on reassembly)
- Lift the plenum up and aside, leaving fuel lines connected
- Cover the open intake runners with shop rags so nothing falls in

On reassembly, replace the intake plenum gasket (one piece, reusable in theory, but cheap enough to replace at 100K).

**Torque is small.** 13 ft-lb is hand-tight plus a quarter turn. The aluminum head will pull threads if you torque this from memory. Use a small in-lb wrench (156 in-lb = 13 ft-lb).
steps: Engine cold. Disconnect negative battery cable.
Pull engine cover (friction fit on 4 grommets).
**Front bank (3 plugs):** Disconnect each coil connector. Remove 10mm coil bolt. Pull coil straight up. Blow compressed air into the plug well to clear debris.
Back the old plug out a half turn with the 14mm thin-wall plug socket and 6" extension. Then turn by hand to feel for cross-threading or stuck threads.
Inspect the old plug — even wear and tan color = good. Erosion = past life or wrong heat range.
Verify the new plug's gap with a wire gauge (don't bend). Apply dielectric grease inside the coil boot.
Thread new plug by hand. If it doesn't go in by hand, stop. Torque to 13 ft-lb (156 in-lb).
Reinstall coil, torque 10mm bolt to 60 in-lb (5 ft-lb). Reconnect harness.
**Rear bank (3 plugs):** Remove throttle body (4 bolts), set aside without disconnecting cooling lines if possible.
Disconnect PCV, EVAP, and brake booster vacuum hoses from the plenum.
Loosen and remove plenum bolts in reverse of torque sequence (consult service manual).
Lift plenum up and toward firewall. Stuff clean rags into the intake runners.
Repeat plug replacement procedure for rear three.
Remove rags. Install new intake plenum gasket. Reinstall plenum, torque bolts in correct sequence (typically center-out, multiple passes).
Reconnect all vacuum lines, throttle body, harnesses. Reconnect battery.
Start, listen for misfire, scan for codes if you have a reader.
pros: 100K mile interval — long service life
Iridium plugs run cleaner than copper on these engines
Front three are quick (15 min)
One job for the next decade on most owners
cons: Rear three require intake plenum removal (2+ hours)
Intake plenum gasket replacement is recommended (extra $25)
Aluminum heads punish overtorque
DIY mistake on the rear bank can damage the intake gasket or drop a bolt into a runner

title: Transfer Case Fluid Change

parts.name: Toyota Genuine 75W Transfer Case Fluid (quart, 3rd gen)

citations.title: Blauparts — Toyota Tacoma transfer case fluid change 2009–2023
Blauparts — Tacoma transfer case fluid types

summary: 2nd gen Tacoma (2005–2015) takes 75W-90 GL-5 in the transfer case; 3rd gen (2016–2023) takes Toyota's specific 75W transfer case fluid; capacity is about 1.05 quarts for both.
description:
The Tacoma transfer case is a chain-driven part-time 4WD unit (RF1A on most years) sitting behind the transmission. It's a low-stress component until you cross water or drive thousands of miles on sealed pavement — both eventually contaminate or thermally degrade the fluid. Toyota's maintenance schedule lists "inspect" rather than a specific change interval, which is too vague for an off-road rig. Plan to drain and refill every 30,000 miles or any time you've been in water deep enough to cover the case.

Fluid choice differs by generation. On 2nd gen (2005–2015) the spec is 75W-90 GL-5 gear oil — the same fluid Toyota uses in the rear differential, and any reputable synthetic 75W-90 works. On 3rd gen (2016–2023) Toyota switched to a thinner 75W transfer case fluid (part 08885-81081). It is not the same fluid as the differentials. Filling a 3rd gen t-case with 75W-90 will technically work but is outside spec; Toyota's own service writers will sometimes do this when 75W is unavailable. For warranty work, stick with 75W. For everything else, decide based on what you can source.

The plugs use a 24mm socket. Fill plug sits high on the rear of the case, drain plug at the bottom. Open the fill plug first — universal rule for any drain-and-fill, and especially important here because the fill plug is angled awkwardly and sometimes seized. Drain into a pan, inspect for metal flakes (a small amount of fine paste is normal; chunks mean the chain is wearing).

Reinstall the drain plug with a fresh crush gasket at 27 ft-lbs. Pump new fluid through the fill until it overflows at the port edge — that's the level. Reinstall the fill plug with a fresh gasket at 27 ft-lbs. Drive the rig and recheck for seepage in a day or two.
steps: Drive 10 minutes to warm the fluid.
Park level on jack stands; chock the front wheels.
Position a drain pan under the transfer case.
Remove the fill plug first with a 24mm socket. Confirm it spins.
Remove the drain plug. Drain fully.
Inspect the drained fluid and any debris on the magnet (if your case has one).
Install a fresh crush gasket on the drain plug. Torque to 27 ft-lbs.
Pump fresh fluid (75W for 3rd gen, 75W-90 GL-5 for 2nd gen) into the fill hole until it overflows.
Install fresh gasket on the fill plug. Torque to 27 ft-lbs.
Recheck for seepage after a short drive.
pros: 30–60 minutes including draining time
Single 24mm socket plus a pump
Catches water intrusion before bearings fail
Cheap insurance compared to a t-case rebuild
cons: 3rd gen requires the specific Toyota 75W fluid — usually a dealer order
Fill plug is at an awkward angle on the upper rear of the case
Crush gaskets are one-use and easy to forget to replace

title: Recovery Gear Starter Kit for the Tacoma

parts.name: ARB Recovery Bag Kit (kinetic rope, snatch block, tree saver, gloves)
Hi-Lift Jack HL-485 (48" cast and steel)

citations.title: ARB Recovery Gear Product Overview
Maxtrax MKII Product Page

summary: A kinetic rope, D-ring shackles, traction boards, and a snatch block cover the majority of recovery scenarios you'll encounter on the trail — and the IFS Tacoma's limited factory recovery points mean you need to address attachment hardware before heading out.
description:
The factory Tacoma front tow hook (2nd gen has a hook mounted to the frame; 3rd gen varies by trim) is functional as a recovery point for straight pulls but is not an appropriate anchor for D-ring shackle attachment without inspection. On some 3rd gen trims the front tow hook is body-mounted rather than frame-mounted — verify yours before using it in a recovery. A steel front bumper with rated D-ring tabs removes all ambiguity. For rear recovery, the receiver hitch is the correct anchor; add a 3/4" D-ring hitch receiver shackle mount ($25–$40) to use it with a kinetic rope.

The kinetic recovery rope is the most important item in this kit. A kinetic (stretchy) rope — like Bubba Rope's 7/8" diameter model — stores and releases energy as a vehicle bounces free, creating a pull that's far more effective than a static strap and much gentler on both vehicles' frames. Static tow straps work in a pinch but they shock-load the recovery points. The kinetic rope is the right tool.

Maxtrax traction boards are the self-recovery solution for when there's no second vehicle. Dig out the tire, slide the Maxtrax under the drive wheels, and drive the truck off them. They work on sand, mud, and snow — the ridged polymer surface grips both the tire and the ground to create traction where the tire has none. They're bulky but worth the space in the bed. The ARB Recovery Kit bundles a kinetic rope, snatch block, tree saver strap, and gloves in a storage bag — it's a solid all-in-one starting point if you don't want to source pieces individually.
steps: Identify and assess your recovery point hardware before loading gear — verify front and rear attachment points are frame-rated
Install D-ring shackle mount in receiver hitch for a rear recovery point if no steel bumper is present
Store kinetic rope in a dedicated bag, away from sharp metal in the bed or cargo area
Mount Hi-Lift to hood-mounted bracket or bed rack — don't store loose in bed where it slides
Carry Maxtrax boards where they can be accessed without unloading the whole bed (many owners mount to the bed rail or roof rack)
Practice recovery scenarios before you need them in the field — know which shackle goes where before you're stuck
After any recovery, inspect all gear: check rope for cuts, D-rings for deformation, and shackle threads for galling
pros: Kinetic rope with a snatch block doubles your effective pull force for vehicle-to-vehicle recovery
Maxtrax provides self-recovery capability when no second vehicle is present
ARB kit bundles the essential components with quality hardware in a single bag
D-ring shackles are universal — work with any vehicle's recovery point
Hi-Lift jack serves triple duty: lifting, winching as a hand winch, and spreading for clamping
cons: IFS Tacoma front recovery points require a steel bumper for reliable D-ring attachment — factory hook varies by trim
Maxtrax boards are expensive per unit; cheaper alternatives exist but with less grip and durability
Recovery gear is only useful if the operator knows proper technique — a kinetic rope attached to a body panel is dangerous
Hi-Lift requires a frame-mounted lift point or bumper notch to use safely — stock bumper is not Hi-Lift compatible
ARB kit does not include a dedicated vehicle-recovery anchor (tree protector strap for anchor use is included, but no ground anchor)

title: Winch for the Tacoma — 9,500 to 12,000 lb Options

parts.name: Warn VR EVO 10-S Winch (10,000 lb, synthetic rope)
Smittybilt X20 10K Winch (10,000 lb, synthetic rope)
Warn M12000-S Winch (12,000 lb, synthetic rope)
Warn Zeon 10-S Winch (10,000 lb, synthetic rope)

citations.title: Warn Winch Selection Guide
Smittybilt X20 Product Page

summary: The Tacoma's GVWR of 4,400–5,500 lbs means a 9,500–10,000 lb winch is the minimum — and a steel front bumper with an integrated winch plate is a prerequisite before the winch itself.
description:
Winch sizing follows a straightforward rule: minimum 1.5x your vehicle's gross vehicle weight rating. The 2nd gen Tacoma GVWR ranges from 4,400 lbs (2WD Access Cab) to 5,500 lbs (4WD Double Cab V6 long bed).
