At the upper end, that's an 8,250 lb minimum — but 9,500 to 10,000 lb is the practical floor because rated line pull is the single-line maximum and real recoveries often add mud suction, wheel spin, and dynamic load. A 10,000 lb winch is the correct size for a loaded Tacoma in typical trail recovery scenarios. A 12,000 lb Warn M12000-S gives meaningful overhead capacity for heavy overlanders or frequent rock crawling.

A winch must mount to a winch plate — a steel mounting interface that transfers pull force through the bumper to the frame. The OEM Tacoma bumper has no winch plate. This means a steel front bumper is not optional if you want to run a winch; it's the prerequisite. Don't mount a winch to a body-mounted winch cradle or DIY plate bolted to the bumper skin — the load path matters and a 10,000 lb pull through an inadequate mount point will deform or tear the body.

Synthetic rope vs steel cable: synthetic rope is the correct choice for trail and overland use. It's lighter, safer when it breaks (falls to the ground rather than snapping back), and easier to handle bare-handed without wire splinters. Steel cable is more abrasion-resistant in extremely rocky terrain but the safety tradeoff isn't worth it for most uses. All four winches listed use synthetic rope as standard.

Electrical: the winch draws 400–500 amps at full load. The power leads must run directly to the battery with the appropriate gauge wire (typically 2/0 AWG for runs under 10 feet). Most winches include the wire in the kit. Route the control cable into the cab for in-cab operation or use the wireless remote that most modern winches include. The wireless remote is a genuine convenience — it lets you stand clear of the line under load.
steps: Install steel front bumper with winch plate before purchasing winch
Verify winch plate dimensions match your chosen winch (most use SAE 10" x 4.5" standard pattern)
Mount winch to winch plate; torque all four mounting bolts to spec (typically 40–50 ft-lb)
Route positive cable from battery to winch; do not connect to battery yet
Route negative cable from winch to a clean chassis ground or battery negative
Route control harness into cab; mount in-cab switch or store wireless remote in accessible location
Connect positive cable to battery last — winch will not spool freely with power connected
Test winch in both directions with no load; verify remote and in-cab controls
Spool out and re-spool the full rope under light tension to seat it evenly on the drum
Test full-load pull against a fixed anchor point before trusting the system in the field
pros: Warn VR EVO 10-S is the best value in serious winches — reliable motor, good speed, backed by Warn's support
Synthetic rope is safer and easier to handle than steel cable in every trail scenario
10,000 lb capacity with a snatch block doubles to 20,000 lb pull — enough for any Tacoma recovery
Wireless remote standard on all modern winches — operate from a safe distance from the line
Warn M12000-S adds meaningful capacity for heavy loads or frequent use without a major price jump
cons: Requires steel front bumper with winch plate — cannot use a winch with the OEM bumper
Smittybilt X20 is a budget option with a weaker motor and less robust internal components — adequate for occasional use, not recommended for frequent or heavy recovery
Winch adds 60–80 lbs to the front of the truck — check front axle weight with a scale if loaded
Synthetic rope can be cut by sharp metal edges on a rock or tight recovery angle — protect rope with a sleeve at any contact point
In-cab wiring adds complexity to the install; improper wire sizing is a fire risk at full-load amp draw

title: Tie Rod Replacement
tools_required: tie rod separator (pickle fork or puller)

parts.name: Toyota OEM Outer Tie Rod End
Toyota OEM Inner Tie Rod Assembly

citations.title: Step-By-Step Outer Tie Rod End Replacement — 2G/3G Tacoma
Tie Rod Ends: 555 vs OEM Discussion — 4Runner Forum
Tacoma Inner Tie Rod Torque Spec
2017 Tacoma Front End Torque Specs

summary: Replace worn Tacoma tie rod ends with 555 (Sankei) or Toyota OEM units; 555 is the same factory supplier as OEM at roughly half the price. Torque outer ends to 67 ft-lbs and count the threads when removing the old ones to preserve alignment.
description:
The Tacoma uses an inner tie rod that threads into the steering rack and an outer tie rod end that attaches to the steering knuckle. Both wear. The outer tie rod end is the one most owners replace first because its ball joint develops play at 80,000-150,000 miles depending on mileage in dirt and salt exposure. Inner tie rods last longer but eventually develop play that you'll feel as on-center wander and a clunking sensation when crossing rough pavement.

The verdict on parts: 555 (Sankei) is what you want unless you have an OEM-or-bust religion. 555 is the actual factory supplier for Toyota inner tie rods on Tacomas and 4Runners. The 555 box and the Toyota box contain functionally the same part. Pay the Toyota markup if you want the Toyota box for warranty reasons; pay for 555 if you want the same part for less. Stay away from no-name imports from chain auto stores — many use looser tolerances on the ball stud and develop play within 20,000 miles.

Moog is also acceptable for Tacoma tie rods, particularly the problem-solver designs that have a grease fitting. Detroit Axle and TRQ have mixed track records — fine for daily drivers, less ideal for trucks running 33s and up.

A critical detail for the outer replacement: count the threads showing on the inner tie rod before removing the old outer, or measure from a fixed point to the lock nut. The new outer needs to be threaded on to the exact same depth or your toe alignment will be off and you'll burn the front tires. An alignment is recommended after any tie rod work, but a careful thread-count measurement gets you home safely and lets you drive to the alignment shop without dragging the tire sideways.

Tacomas pull the right side outer tie rod first more often than the left because of cambered roads and the way the steering geometry loads. If only one side is bad, replace both anyway — the other side is on a similar timeline and you don't want this job again in six months.
steps: Loosen the front lug nuts. Jack the front of the truck, set jack stands under the frame, and pull both front wheels.
For an outer tie rod swap: count the threads visible between the inner tie rod boot and the outer tie rod end. Photograph for reference.
Crack the lock nut where the outer threads onto the inner tie rod (21mm). Do not fully back it off yet.
Pull the cotter pin from the castle nut on the outer ball stud. Remove the castle nut (19mm).
Separate the outer tie rod from the steering knuckle using a tie rod puller or pickle fork. Pickle forks tear the boot — only use one if you're replacing the part anyway.
Unscrew the outer tie rod from the inner shaft, counting turns.

Thread the new outer onto the inner the same number of turns. Reinstall through the steering knuckle. Torque castle nut to 67 ft-lbs, then advance to the nearest cotter pin hole and install a new cotter pin.
Snug the lock nut against the new outer at 35-40 ft-lbs.
For inner tie rod replacement: remove the outer first (above), then pull the rack boot clamps off and slide the boot back to expose the inner.
Use an inner tie rod removal tool (purchasable or rentable) to break the inner loose from the rack. Inner torque from factory is high — expect to put real force into it.
Thread the new inner in. Torque inner to 60 ft-lbs against the rack housing.
Slide the boot back, install new clamps, reinstall the outer, and torque to spec.
Reinstall wheels. Torque lug nuts to 83 ft-lbs.
Drive directly to an alignment shop. Toe is the alignment angle most affected by tie rod work and the only one you can't eyeball.
pros: 555 brand is the same factory supplier — half the cost of Toyota-boxed OEM
Restores tight on-center steering feel that mileage steals slowly
Outer-only replacement is a one-hour job per side
cons: Outer ball stud is corroded into the knuckle on rust-belt trucks and may require heat to release
Inner tie rod requires a dedicated tool to remove cleanly
Alignment is mandatory after — budget the shop visit into the job

title: Budget Lift Kit — Coilovers and Add-a-Leaf (≤$600)

parts.name: Bilstein B8 6112 Front Coilover Pair (2005-2023 Tacoma)

citations.title: Bilstein 6112 Installation Guide
Tacoma World — Budget Lift Discussion

summary: A Bilstein 6112 front coilover set paired with a quality rear add-a-leaf is the most capable budget lift option for the Tacoma — 1.5"–2" of lift, meaningfully better damping, and the foundation to go further if your build evolves.
description:
The Tacoma's IFS front end responds well to a quality coilover even at the budget tier. The Bilstein 6112 is a height-adjustable strut that replaces the OEM spring-shock assembly in one unit. At full compression it delivers around 1.5"–2" of lift over stock without compromising ride quality the way a cheap spacer lift will. The rear add-a-leaf packs that pair well with this setup — OME Dakar or SCS — add progressive spring rate and lift the rear 1"–1.5" to keep the truck level.

What this tier does not give you is additional wheel travel or corrected CV joint angles. At 2" of lift the front CV shafts are operating near their design limits. If you're planning anything above 2" — or running aggressive terrain where the suspension cycles fully — upper control arms become necessary to restore caster geometry and reduce stress on the ball joints. Skipping UCAs and stacking more lift on top of the 6112s is a path to premature ball joint and CV wear. At the ≤$600 price point, the right call is to stay at 1.5"–2" and plan UCAs as the next upgrade.

The 6112 is height-adjustable via a threaded collar, which lets you dial in the front height precisely. Set the rear first by measuring loaded ride height, then match the front to achieve a slight nose-up rake (1/4"–1/2" front lower than rear when loaded) for a planted trail feel. Torque all suspension fasteners with the vehicle at ride height — not in the air — to avoid binding the rubber bushings at full droop.
steps: Chock rear wheels, break front lug nuts loose before lifting
Lift front of truck, support on jack stands at the frame rails
Remove front wheel and tire
Disconnect sway bar end link from strut
Remove brake line bracket from strut housing
Mark OEM strut-to-knuckle pinch bolt orientation before removing
Remove upper strut mount nuts from engine bay
Remove strut-to-knuckle pinch bolts and slide strut out
Set 6112 coilover collar to desired lift height per Bilstein's height chart
Install 6112 into knuckle, torque pinch bolts to spec (148 ft-lb for most years)
Reinstall upper mount nuts and torque to spec
Reconnect brake line bracket and sway bar end link
Repeat opposite side
Move to rear: lift rear of truck, support at frame
Remove rear wheels
Support rear axle under differential housing with a jack
Disconnect rear sway bar end links
Lower axle slightly to create leaf spring access
Remove U-bolts and lower spring plate
Insert add-a-leaf into the pack per manufacturer's stacking order
Reassemble spring pack, install new U-bolts if provided, torque to spec
Reinstall wheels, lower truck, bounce suspension to settle
Torque all suspension fasteners at ride height
Get an alignment — caster and camber will be affected
pros: Best bang for $300–$600 in the Tacoma suspension budget
Bilstein 6112 is significantly better than OEM damping for trail and highway
Add-a-leaf rear increases load capacity slightly, useful for overlanders carrying gear
Height-adjustable front allows precise leveling
No alignment camber issues at 1.5"–2" lift
Maintains full IFS warranty-adjacent geometry at this lift height
cons: Does not address CV angle or caster — UCAs needed for anything above 2"
Add-a-leaf stiffens the rear spring rate; ride quality on pavement is firmer
No additional wheel travel compared to stock — bump and droop are unchanged
Budget rear add-a-leaf packs vary in quality; SCS is fine for mild use, OME Dakar is the better long-term choice
Does not fit 285/75R16 (33") tires without trimming at this lift height — 32" tires are the safe maximum

title: Coilover Replacement — Bilstein 6112 / Icon / Fox

parts.name: Bilstein 6112 Front Coilover Kit (3rd Gen Tacoma, 2016-2023)
Bilstein 5160 Rear Reservoir Shocks (3rd Gen Tacoma)
Bilstein 6112 Front Coilover Kit (2nd Gen Tacoma, 2005-2015)
Fox 2.5 Performance Series Coilover (DSC adjuster optional)

citations.title: Bilstein 6112 2" Lift System — 16-23 Tacoma
Bilstein 6112 Kit for 2005-2015 Tacoma
Bilstein 47-310896 Front 6112 Kit Tacoma 1996-2004

summary: Bilstein 6112 coilovers give the Tacoma a 0–2.5" front lift with better damping than the stock-tuned-soft units, in a pre-assembled bolt-in package matched to either 2nd gen (2005-2015) or 3rd gen (2016-2023) trucks.
description:
Stock Tacoma front coilover struts are valved for unloaded daily driving. Add a bumper, skid plate, and a few weekend trips and the front sags 0.5"–1" below stock, with brake-dive on every stop and float over washboard. The 6112 is the go-to upgrade: 60mm piston, snap-ring-adjustable spring perch, pre-assembled with a Bilstein-tuned coil.

The 6112 ships with multiple perch positions giving 0", 0.5", 1.25", 1.85", and 2.5" of front lift. Most owners run position 3 (around 1.25"–1.85") which clears 265/75R16 or 275/70R17 tires without CV-angle problems. Going to the top position (2.5"+) stresses CV axles — budget for shorter CV life or pair with a diff drop.

Three upgrade tiers. Tier 1: Bilstein 6112 front + 5160 rear ($820 + $425). Best damping-per-dollar; bolt-in; rebuildable rear shocks. Tier 2: Icon Stage 2 ($1950 matched kit). Better damping curve, dual-rate spring, threaded body for fine-tune adjustment, longer service intervals. Tier 3: Fox 2.5 Performance Series with optional DSC adjuster ($1450+). Race-grade damping with on-the-fly compression adjustability — overkill for daily driving, perfect for desert work.

Add-a-leaf or full leaf-pack replacement at the rear is a separate decision. The Icon 1.5" add-a-leaf works for mild trail and overlanding load; for heavier loads or rougher trails, go to a full Deaver or Icon leaf pack instead.

Install mirrors the 4Runner procedure. Break the upper ball joint or remove the UCA, separate the tie rod end, drop the lower strut bolt. No spring compressor needed — the 6112 ships fully assembled. Critical torque values: upper strut nuts 47 ft-lb; lower strut bolt 100 ft-lb at ride height; tie rod castle nut 67 ft-lb; upper ball joint nut 80 ft-lb. Always tighten the lower strut bolt with the suspension loaded (at ride height) to prevent bushing pre-load. Alignment is mandatory after.

For 2nd gen Tacomas (2005-2015), the 6112 part number is different (47-309975) but the install procedure matches. Pre-2005 Tacomas use a different platform entirely; see the dedicated 1st gen Tacoma guide if applicable.
steps: Park on level ground; loosen front lug nuts.
Lift the front; support the frame on jack stands; remove the front wheels.
Disconnect the sway bar end links from the lower control arms.
Separate the tie rod end from the steering knuckle.
Remove the upper ball joint nut and pop the UCA free (or remove the UCA entirely for clearance).
Support the lower control arm with a floor jack.
Remove three upper strut nuts from the strut tower.
Remove the lower strut bolt at the LCA.
Drop the old strut down and out.
Install the new 6112 at your chosen perch position.
Snug upper nuts; install lower bolt loosely.
Load the LCA with the floor jack to ride height, then torque the lower bolt to 100 ft-lb.
Torque upper strut nuts to 47 ft-lb.
Reconnect tie rod (67 ft-lb), upper ball joint (80 ft-lb), sway bar end links.
Repeat the other side.
Reinstall wheels; torque lug nuts to 83 ft-lb.
Drive directly to alignment shop.
pros: Best damping upgrade per dollar in the Tacoma aftermarket
Five lift positions on a single coilover — tune after install
Pre-assembled; no spring compressor
Works on 2nd or 3rd gen with platform-specific part numbers
cons: Above 1.85" lift, CV axles wear faster
Alignment required immediately after install
Upper control arms become a recommended companion above 2"
6112 valving is fixed — Fox 2.5 with DSC or Icon adjustable required for tunability

title: Heavy Leaf Pack Upgrade — Deaver / OME / Icon

parts.name: Deaver U402 Stage I (pair) — 0-300 lb bed load
Old Man Emu Dakar EL112R heavy load leaf (single)
Icon RXT Multi-Rate Leaf Pack with add-in
U-bolt and hardware kit (always replace U-bolts)

citations.title: Deaver Tacoma Expedition Spring
Icon RXT Tacoma Leaf Pack
OME EL112R Heavy Load Leaf
AdventureTaco — Replacing Leaf Springs on a Tacoma

summary: If you're carrying a rooftop tent, drawer system, fridge, water, and fuel, the stock Tacoma rear leaf pack will sag and ride harshly within the first year — Deaver, OME Dakar, and Icon RXT each fix this differently, and the right choice depends on how much weight you actually carry.
description:
The stock Tacoma rear leaf pack is tuned for an empty bed. Add 300+ lbs of overland gear and the truck sags, the ride goes from firm to harsh-and-bouncy (because the spring rate is wrong for the new loaded weight), and the rear axle wraps under throttle. Adding a leaf to the stock pack with an "AAL" (Add-A-Leaf) helps slightly, but it's a band-aid. A complete replacement pack is the durable fix.

**Deaver** builds custom packs by load. The Stage I (U402) is the most popular Tacoma leaf — 9 leaves, 2" lift, rated for 0-300 lb constant bed load. Stage II handles 300-600 lb (camper shell, drawers, fuel cans). Stage III handles 600+ lb (slide-in campers). Deaver ride quality is the benchmark: smoother than stock when loaded, stays planted unloaded. About $680-$750 per pair.

**Old Man Emu Dakar** is the value option at roughly $580 for the EL097R (medium) or $620 for the EL112R (heavy) per pair. About 2.25" of lift. Stiffer than Deaver but built for global expedition duty — the parts are everywhere and you can order them anywhere. Best fit for moderate loads with occasional heavy days.

**Icon RXT Multi-Rate** uses a progressive-rate pack with tip inserts and leaf separators to reduce friction. Around $920-$1,000 per pair. Best ride quality of the three when unloaded, holds well loaded. The premium choice if budget allows.

What to avoid: cheap Add-A-Leaf kits ($120-$180). They wedge an extra leaf into the stock pack, which alters the arc and stresses the main leaf. Lift comes from preload, not from a redesigned pack. Most owners regret AALs within a year.

All three require new U-bolts (always — never reuse). Plan to do shackles and bushings at the same time, especially on a 2nd gen with 100k+ miles. Pinion angle will change with the new lift; check with a digital level and add a degreed shim if vibration shows up over 50 mph.
steps: Park on level ground, chock the front wheels, jack the rear, set on stands under the frame.
Support the rear axle with a floor jack to prevent it dropping when bolts come out.
Soak shackle bolts, U-bolt nuts, and front leaf eye bolt with penetrating oil. These are seized on most trucks.
Loosen U-bolt nuts on top of the axle. Remove the U-bolt plate and U-bolts.
Disconnect the rear shackle (one bolt). Lower the rear of the spring.
Remove the front eye bolt. The spring drops out.
Compare new pack to old — leaf count, arc, eye position. Confirm match.
Install new pack: front eye first, hand-thread bolt; then shackle, hand-thread bolt.
Use new U-bolts. Torque U-bolts to 90 ft-lb in crisscross pattern.
Front eye bolt and shackle bolts: torque to 110 ft-lb **with vehicle weight on the wheels** (lower it first).
Repeat for the other side.
Drive 50 miles to settle the springs. Re-check torque on U-bolts. Get an alignment.
pros: Eliminates sag with overland load
Restores correct spring rate for loaded weight
Deaver is custom-tuned to your actual cargo
Icon RXT progressive-rate rides best unloaded
cons: $580-$1,400 depending on brand
Premium packs are heavier than stock — expect a slight unloaded MPG hit
U-bolts and shackle bolts often seize and require heat
Pinion angle may need correction with a degreed shim
Alignment required after install

title: Rear Leaf Spring Replacement and Add-a-Leaf

parts.name: OME Dakar CS047R rear leaf springs (2nd gen)
OME Dakar CS048RA rear springs (3rd gen)
Deaver Stage I rear pack (0-300 lb load)

citations.title: Replacing Leaf Springs on a Tacoma — AdventureTaco
Buyer's Guide: Leaf Springs For 2nd & 3rd Gen Tacoma
Deaver Toyota Tacoma 05-23 Rear Leaf Spring Kit

summary: Add-a-leaf for under $150 if you only need a small lift and you carry no real weight. Full replacement pack — OME Dakar around $400 or Deaver Stage I/II around $950–$1,100 — if you carry a topper, camper, drawer system, or bumper. Tacomas sag, and an add-a-leaf is a band-aid on a load problem.
description:
The Tacoma's stock rear leaf pack is famous for two things: it rides like a buckboard when empty, and it sags badly the moment you carry any real weight. 2nd gen (2005–2015) and 3rd gen (2016–2023) both share this characteristic, though Toyota issued a TSB and revised the post-TSB packs around 2012. There are three ways to address it: an add-a-leaf, a replacement pack, or a custom progressive pack.

An add-a-leaf is a single extra leaf you bolt into the existing stock pack. Icon, OME, Deaver, and others all sell them in the $120–$200 range. With factory loads, an add-a-leaf yields about 1.5 inches of lift. It stiffens the existing pack and slows future sag but doesn't really fix the underlying issue — the leaves underneath are still tired stock leaves. Add-a-leaf is the right answer if you're on a tight budget, your stock pack is still in good shape, and you're not carrying a topper or camper. It's the wrong answer if your stock pack already has visible reverse arch.

A full replacement pack is the right answer for anyone running real overland gear. OME Dakar (about $400 per side equivalent, often sold as a pair around $400–$500) is the budget overlander's standard — about 2.5 to 2.75 inches of lift, designed for around 250 lb constant load, decent ride empty. Deaver offers three stages keyed to constant bed weight: Stage I (0–300 lb), Stage II (400–600 lb), and Stage III (700–1,000 lb). Deaver's 9-leaf and 10-leaf progressive packs run thinner individual leaves that yield a smoother spring curve through the full suspension cycle — that progressive rate is why people who can afford Deavers run them. Plan on $950–$1,100 for the Deaver pack, plus shocks rated for the new lift height (Bilstein 5100, 5160, or Icon 2.0).

Either way, factor in the consumables. The U-bolts that clamp the pack to the axle are one-time-use; budget $50–$80 for new ones. The shackle bushings are usually shot if the truck has 100k+ miles, and new poly or rubber bushings are cheap insurance. The center pin that locates the pack on the axle is tiny and grade-8 — check it. And in any rust state (Phoenix-spec Tacomas are usually fine, Northeast trucks are not), soak every bolt for 24 hours with penetrant before you swing a wrench, because shearing a leaf spring eye bolt on a rusted axle is a tow-truck-level mistake.
steps: Park on a flat surface, chock the front wheels, and break rear lug nuts loose.
Lift the rear, support the frame on jack stands, and let the axle hang on a second floor jack under the diff.
Disconnect the rear shocks at the lower mounts.
Disconnect the parking brake cable bracket and the rear brake hard line bracket from the axle if they interfere.
Remove the U-bolts. Lower the axle slightly to relax the leaf pack.
Remove the rear shackle bolts, then the front spring eye bolt.
Pull the old pack out. Inspect bushings and shackle plates; replace as needed.
Install the new pack. Engage the center pin in the axle perch.
Install new U-bolts with the supplied or grade-8 nuts. Torque per manufacturer spec.
Reconnect shocks, brake lines, parking brake cable. Lower truck to ride height.
Final torque all bolts at ride height. Re-check after 100 miles.
pros: Full pack replacement fixes load capacity, not just height
Deaver progressive packs ride better empty than stock
OME Dakar is the budget overlander default
Add-a-leaf is a 2-hour, $150 fix for mild needs
cons: Rust-belt Tacomas turn a 3-hour job into a 12-hour job
Add-a-leaf doesn't fix tired underlying leaves
Stiffer pack rides harshly when empty
New U-bolts and shackle hardware add to the parts cost

title: Long-Travel Suspension — Expedition and Desert Build ($2,500+)
tools_required: welder or access to fab shop

parts.name: Total Chaos Fabrication Long-Travel Suspension Kit (Tacoma 2005-2023)
Icon Vehicle Dynamics 2.5 VS Remote Reservoir Coilover Kit (Tacoma)
Fox 2.5 Factory Series Remote Reservoir Coilovers (Tacoma)
King OEM Performance+ Remote Reservoir Coilovers (Tacoma)

citations.title: Total Chaos Long-Travel Kit Documentation
Icon Vehicle Dynamics 2.5 VS RR Product Page

summary: Long-travel suspension transforms the Tacoma from a capable trail truck into a high-speed desert runner — 12"+ of wheel travel, 3"–4" of lift, and the ability to carry speed over rough terrain that would bottom out a standard-travel build.
description:
Long-travel suspension is not an upgrade — it's a platform rebuild. A Total Chaos long-travel kit replaces the entire front suspension geometry with extended lower control arms, relocated shock mounts, extended UCAs, and a wider front track. The result is 12"–14" of front wheel travel versus the 8"–9" of a standard IFS Tacoma. Combined with 2.5" remote reservoir or bypass coilovers, the truck handles high-speed desert trails, wash crossings, and rocky terrain with a composure no stock-geometry build can match.

The practical tradeoff is complexity. Long-travel kits typically require cutting the inner fender well and sometimes the subframe to accommodate the wider lower control arm sweep. Many installs require a mild amount of fabrication — removing OEM brackets, adding bumpstop extensions, and occasionally welding new mount tabs. This is not a first lift project. Most owners bring the truck to a reputable 4x4 shop for the long-travel install even if they're comfortable doing mid-tier suspension work themselves.

Shock selection defines the tier. Icon 2.5 VS Remote Reservoir coilovers ($2,299 pair front) are the entry point for remote reservoir damping — they offer external compression adjustment and hold fluid temperature better than internal-bypass units on repeated hits. Fox 2.5 Factory Series ($1,899) are comparable. If the budget stretches to external bypass shocks (Fox 2.5 x 4.0 bypass, $3,500+), the damping becomes position-sensitive — soft in the mid-stroke for small chop, firm at the limits to prevent bottoming. That's true high-desert performance territory.

Rear setup matters as much as front on a long-travel build. Most desert-oriented Tacomas replace the leaf springs with a 4-link coilover rear conversion for matching wheel travel — that's another $2,000–$4,000. The total system cost for a complete long-travel front-and-rear build with quality bypass shocks often exceeds $8,000 before wheels, tires, and alignment.
steps: Document stock dimensions: front track width, ride height at all four corners, caster angle
Order complete kit including extended UCAs, lower control arms, shock mounts, and coilovers
Lift front of truck fully; support on jack stands at frame rails
Remove front wheels, brake calipers (hang — do not stress brake lines), rotors
Disconnect sway bar end links and sway bar from frame
Remove OEM lower control arm, spindle, hub assembly, and upper control arm
Mark and cut inner fender per kit manufacturer templates (Total Chaos kits include patterns)
Install new lower control arm brackets per kit — these typically require grade 8 hardware and specific torque sequences
Install extended lower control arms and set pivot hardware snug
Install new spindle/hub assembly with extended UCAs
Mount coilover: upper in new position, lower to LCA. Set preload and ride height per shock manufacturer spec
Install bumpstop extensions — critical to prevent coilover bottoming
Reconnect sway bar or install long-travel sway bar end links
Reinstall brakes and wheels
Complete rear suspension: install new leaf pack, extended shocks, or coilover conversion if doing full rear upgrade
Lower vehicle, bounce to settle, perform preliminary torque check
Drive to alignment shop; request extended-travel spec alignment — may need adjustable toe and caster plates
Break in shocks per manufacturer spec (typically 500 miles before recheck and valve adjustment)
Recheck all fasteners at 100 miles and 500 miles
pros: 12"–14" of front wheel travel — the most capable IFS Tacoma front end available
Handles high-speed desert terrain and aggressive trail obstacles that standard builds cannot
Remote reservoir coilovers stay cooler on repeated suspension cycles — no fade on desert runs
Wide front track improves stability on off-camber trails
Foundation for a serious overland or desert racing build
cons: Inner fender cutting is irreversible — commits the truck to this platform
Requires alignment shop familiar with extended-travel Toyota geometry
Install complexity demands fabrication skills or a shop — not a weekend driveway job for most owners
Wider track can cause fender contact on street driving if fenders are not trimmed or flared
Full system cost including rear conversion approaches $8,000–$12,000 for a complete build
Overkill for anything short of regular high-speed desert running or competitive trail use

title: Lower Ball Joint Replacement — 1st and 2nd Gen
tools_required: pickle fork or tie rod separator

parts.name: Harbor Freight Ball Joint Press Set

citations.title: Step-by-Step Replacing Lower Ball Joints (1st Gen Tacoma)
Toyota Lower Ball Joint Recall information
Lower Ball Joint Press Receiver Second Gen
Tacoma torque specs: lower ball joint & CV

summary: Tacoma lower ball joints are press-fit into the lower control arm and require a proper press kit — do not skip the press; this is a safety-critical joint, and a 2001–2004 recall (NHTSA 06V-249) makes ball joint provenance worth checking before you install used parts.
description:
The Tacoma uses a press-fit lower ball joint that lives in a cup formed into the lower control arm. A castellated nut on top holds the knuckle on the joint stud. When the joint is worn, you'll hear a knocking at low speed over driveway lips, see uneven inner tire wear, or find play when prying between the LCA and the knuckle. A worn lower ball joint can separate without warning at speed — this is the failure mode behind the 2001–2004 Toyota recall, where joints exited the lower control arm and the front wheel folded under the truck.

OEM Toyota (43330-09780 for 2nd gen) is the right part. The 555 brand from Japan ($65) is the same supplier that builds OEM joints for Toyota and is a legitimate budget option. Moog K500036 ($55) is the U.S. aftermarket pick and includes a grease zerk that OEM omits — useful for trucks that see water crossings. Avoid no-name parts and any joint without a clear country of origin.

Second-gen Tacomas (2005–2015) require a specific receiver cup sized for the larger joint body. The Harbor Freight ball joint press kit ($60) covers most cases, but 2nd gen may need an extra receiver from a separate adapter set or a rented cup from a parts store. Confirm fit before you start the job. A shop press with the right cups is faster and safer than the in-vehicle press for the install side.

The job is best done with the lower control arm out of the truck. Pull the LCA, take it to a press, and swap the joint on a bench. Trying to do it in-vehicle on a 2nd gen leaves you working at awkward angles with the CV axle in the way.
steps: Loosen lug nuts, jack up front, support frame on stands, remove wheel.
Disconnect the lower shock mount, the sway bar end link, and the tie rod from the knuckle.
Remove the cotter pin and castellated nut from the lower ball joint stud (24mm on 2nd gen).
Separate the lower ball joint from the knuckle with a pickle fork or tie rod separator.
Unbolt the LCA cam bolts (mark cam positions first with paint to preserve alignment) and remove the LCA.
Press the old ball joint out on a bench press using the receiver cup that matches the joint body.
Press the new joint in until fully seated against the LCA cup shoulder.
Reinstall LCA, return cam bolts to marked positions, torque LCA cam bolts to 100 ft-lbs.
Install the knuckle on the joint, torque the castellated nut to 67 ft-lbs, then advance to the next cotter pin slot.
Reconnect shock, sway bar link, and tie rod. Torque the tie rod castellated nut to 67 ft-lbs.
Get a rack alignment — cam bolts move during install no matter how carefully you mark them.
pros: OEM-quality joint lasts 100,000+ miles
Restores a safety-critical front-end component
Press kits make the bench install fast
cons: 2nd gen requires the right receiver cup
Job demands a press — no shortcuts
Always get a rack alignment after — wandering cam bolts will eat tires

title: Mid-Tier Lift with Upper Control Arms ($600–$2,000)

parts.name: Icon Vehicle Dynamics Stage 2 Complete Lift Kit (Tacoma 2005-2023)
Total Chaos Fabrication Billet UCA Kit (Tacoma)

citations.title: Icon Vehicle Dynamics Stage 2 Kit Documentation
Total Chaos Fabrication UCA Install Guide

summary: The mid-tier lift is where the Tacoma platform actually opens up — 2.5"–3" of lift, corrected caster and CV geometry from quality UCAs, and enough clearance for 33" tires without rubbing.
description:
At 2.5" of lift and above, the factory upper control arms become a liability. The OEM UCAs were designed for stock ride height — at 2.5"+, the ball joint angle steepens, the CV shaft operates at an angle that accelerates wear, and the factory caster is lost, which creates vague steering and highway wander. Upper control arms solve all three problems simultaneously: they restore caster, raise the outer ball joint to correct CV angle, and provide more droop travel than stock.

Icon's Stage 2 kit bundles everything you need — front coilovers, rear shocks, rear add-a-leaf, and Icon's billet aluminum UCAs. It's the easiest path to a complete mid-tier build because the components are spec'd to work together. If you prefer a la carte, Total Chaos UCAs paired with Bilstein 6112 fronts and OME Dakar leafs in the rear delivers comparable geometry at a similar price with arguably better long-travel potential if you upgrade shocks later.

SPC Performance UCAs are the budget UCA option — they're adjustable (camber and caster eccentric bolts) and work well for street-focused builds. For aggressive trail use or frequent off-road cycling, Total Chaos billet units are the more durable choice; the SPC arms use an OEM-style stamped design with aftermarket adjustability rather than a full billet rebuild. Camburg UCAs ($849) sit between the two in both price and construction quality.

Do not skip the alignment after this install. A mid-lift with UCAs will set new caster and camber positions that require a proper alignment to dial in. Most shops familiar with Tacoma builds can hit +3.5° caster and 0° camber, which gives neutral highway feel. Budget the alignment as part of the project cost.
steps: Plan the build: confirm UCA brand, shock/coilover spec, and rear setup before ordering
Lift front of vehicle, support on jack stands, remove front wheels
Disconnect sway bar end links and brake line brackets
Remove front strut assembly (both sides)
Remove OEM upper control arm — disconnect ball joint from spindle, remove UCA bolts from frame
Install new UCA per manufacturer instructions; torque frame bolts to spec but leave snug, not final torque (set at ride height)
Install new coilovers or struts; set height collar to target lift (typically position 3 of 6 on threaded collar)
Reconnect ball joint to spindle with new nut; torque to spec (typically 90–100 ft-lb)
Reconnect sway bar end links and brake line brackets
Reinstall wheels
Move to rear: remove wheels, support axle
Remove U-bolts and spring plate; install rear shocks if included in kit
Install rear add-a-leaf or replace full leaf pack per kit instructions
Reassemble rear, torque U-bolts to spec
Lower vehicle to ride height
Final torque all suspension fasteners with vehicle at ride height
Drive to alignment shop within 50 miles; request Tacoma-specific caster/camber specs
After alignment, test drive on varied terrain and recheck torque at 500 miles
pros: Corrected caster and CV geometry — the core reason to do this tier over budget lift
Fits 285/75R16 (33") tires cleanly on most 3rd gen Tacomas; some trimming on 2nd gen
Significantly improved wheel travel over stock — especially with coilovers at this tier
Icon Stage 2 kit eliminates component compatibility guesswork
UCAs extend the life of ball joints and CV shafts at lifted heights
Adjustable coilover height allows fine-tuning later without buying new springs
cons: Requires a professional alignment after install — budget $100–$150 additional
Substantially more complex than budget lift; ball joint press required for UCA swap
SPC UCAs are adjustable but not as robust as billet alternatives for heavy trail use
3rd gen Tacoma (2016+) has more clearance for 33s; 2nd gen may need minor trimming of front mudflap bracket
Does not deliver long-travel performance — suspension still cycles through OEM-range bump and droop

title: Upper Control Arm Upgrade After Lift — 3rd Gen Tacoma
tools_required: pickle fork or ball joint separator

parts.name: Dirt King Ball Joint UCAs Tacoma

citations.title: Total Chaos UCAs For Tacoma — Install/Review (TrailTacoma)
13 Best Upper Control Arms For Tacoma — TrailTacoma
Upper and Lower Control Arms — Tacoma3G Forum

summary: A 3rd gen Tacoma with more than 2 inches of front lift will run out of caster before the alignment cams do — adjustable UCAs put caster back where Toyota specced it and stop the truck from wandering on the freeway.
description:
The 3rd gen Tacoma uses the same double-wishbone IFS layout as the 4Runner, with a longer wheelbase and different spindle. The geometry behaves the same: lift the front, the UCA rotates down at the ball joint, caster goes negative. Toyota specs front caster around +2.3° to +3.5°. After a 2.5" lift on stock arms, expect it to land near 0° to +1°. Highway behavior degrades — the truck darts at lane changes, doesn't return to center after a turn, and feels heavy in your hands at 70 mph.

Brand options on Tacoma are slightly wider than the 4Runner because aftermarket Tacoma is the larger market. SPC ($600–$700) is the sealed ball joint budget choice and works for daily drivers who want their truck to drive like a Toyota again. Total Chaos sells two versions — a urethane bushing version ($650) and a uniball version ($850) — and the urethane is the right pick for a mostly-on-road truck. Camburg's billet UCAs ($900–$1000) use Heim joints at the pivot and add 2° of caster via spacer orientation, which is the trick high-clearance long-travel builders look for. Dirt King's ball joint version mirrors SPC at a similar price.

Don't confuse "caster correction" with "more travel." Adjustable UCAs recover the caster you lost from lifting — they don't add wheel travel by themselves. You'll get a small bonus in droop (around 0.5"–1") from the higher-misalignment ball joint or uniball, but that's not the reason to install them. If you want real travel, you're in long-travel-kit territory with new lower arms and extended coilovers, and that's a different conversation.

Uniball wear is real. A daily-driven Tacoma with uniball UCAs will start clunking over speed bumps at 30K–40K miles. The fix is a uniball rebuild — Total Chaos sells the rebuild kit for around $50 per side. If clunking on a stock-vehicle drive bothers you, get the urethane bushing version from Total Chaos or the sealed ball joint version from SPC or Dirt King. The 1st gen Tacoma SPC arms are not the same as the 3rd gen — make sure you order the right generation.

After install, the alignment is mandatory. Target caster: +2.5° to +3.5°. Higher caster (3.5°+) gives stable highway tracking but heavier steering feel; lower caster (2.0°–2.5°) gives lighter, quicker steering. Set camber to 0° to +0.25° and toe to Toyota spec (front 0° to 0.10° in).
steps: Park on level ground, chock rear wheels.
Loosen front lug nuts. Lift the front of the truck, support on stands under the frame.
Remove front wheel.
Support the lower control arm with a floor jack to keep the coilover loaded.
Disconnect ABS sensor wire and brake hose bracket from the stock UCA.
Pull the upper ball joint cotter pin, loosen the castle nut.
Separate the upper ball joint from the spindle with a pickle fork or ball joint press.
Remove the two UCA pivot bolts at the frame (19mm).
Pull the stock UCA out.
Install the new UCA. Torque pivot bolts to factory spec (87 ft-lb for the front bolt, 101 ft-lb for the rear bolt).
Slot the new ball joint into the spindle, torque the nut per kit instructions (typically 60–80 ft-lb), install cotter pin.
Re-route brake hose and ABS wire onto the new arm's bracket.
Reinstall the wheel, lug nuts to 83 ft-lb.
Lower the truck.
Get a four-wheel alignment. Caster target: +2.5° to +3.5°.
pros: Restores factory caster after a 2"+ lift
Stops freeway wandering and vague return-to-center
Bolt-in install — no frame mods
Pick a sealed ball joint version (SPC, Dirt King) or urethane Total Chaos for a quiet daily driver
Small droop bonus on uniball versions
cons: Uniball versions clunk after 30K–50K and need rebuilding
$600–$1000 is a lot to add to a lift budget you already spent
1st gen Tacoma UCAs don't fit 3rd gen — check generation before ordering
Alignment after install is required, not optional

title: Running 33" Tires on the Tacoma — 285/75R16 and 295/70R17 Fitment

citations.title: Tacoma World Tire Fitment Guide
BFGoodrich KO2 Product Specifications

summary: 285/75R16 (33.8" diameter) is the sweet spot for the lifted Tacoma — fits on 2" of lift with minor trimming of the front mud flap bracket, runs cleanly on 2.5"+ lift, and delivers meaningful off-road capability over the stock 265s.
description:
The 285/75R16 measures 33.8" in actual diameter on most brands — slightly taller than the commonly referenced "33s" designation. On a 2" lifted Tacoma, these tires will contact the front mudflap bracket under full compression and full lock. Trimming that plastic bracket — a 10-minute job with a razor knife — eliminates the rub. On 2.5"+ of lift they run cleanly without any modification. The 295/70R17 (33.5" diameter) is the 17" equivalent; it needs a minimum of 2.5" lift for clean clearance and 3"+ on the 2nd gen Tacoma's narrower front fender opening.

For 2nd gen Tacomas (2005–2015), the inner fender liner can contact 285/75R16 at full compression on aggressive terrain. Pulling the liner slightly inward or trimming the leading edge of the liner prevents this. It's a minor fix but worth doing before trail use. The 3rd gen (2016–2023) has a slightly wider front opening and handles 285/75R16 more gracefully, often with zero trimming at 2.5" of lift.

Tire selection matters as much as size. The BFG KO2 remains the benchmark all-terrain option — balanced street manners, proven off-road traction, and long tread life. The Falken Wildpeak AT3W punches above its price point for wet traction and rock grip. Toyo's Open Country AT3 is quieter on-road with comparable off-road performance. If the build is trail-focused over pavement-focused, the Nitto Ridge Grappler (a hybrid AT/MT pattern) in 285/75R16 is worth considering.

At 33" diameter, the Tacoma's speedometer will read approximately 3–4% low with stock gear ratios on a 2nd or 3rd gen. This does not require a re-gear unless you're towing heavily or adding 35s. If you're running 33s and noticing labored acceleration or slipping between gears on highway climbs, check the final drive ratio against the tire diameter using a gear ratio calculator before committing to a re-gear.
steps: Confirm current lift height and clearance with a measuring tape before ordering tires
Order tires and wheels; verify wheel backspacing suits lift height (4.75"–5" backspacing for 2.5"+ lift)
Mount tires to wheels at a tire shop; request TPMS sensor transfer if applicable
Install wheels with vehicle on jack stands; torque lug nuts to 85 ft-lb in a star pattern
Test drive at low speed and check for rub at full lock before hitting the trail
Trim front mudflap bracket if 285/75R16 contacts on 2" lift (plastic — razor knife or jigsaw)
Trim inner fender liner on 2nd gen if needed — pull back the liner and mark contact point
Recheck lug torque at 50 miles after new wheel/tire install
pros: 285/75R16 is the widest common size that fits on a 2" lift with minor trimming
Substantially better trail traction than factory 265s — taller sidewall absorbs trail chop
Wide variety of quality AT and MT options in this size from every major brand
6-ply sidewall on most 33" AT tires resists punctures and sidewall cuts
No gear ratio change required for normal trail and street use
cons: 285/75R16 on 2" lift requires mudflap bracket trim — minor but necessary
295/70R17 needs 2.5"+ lift minimum; too tight on 2nd gen at 2"
Taller tires increase rotational mass — minor reduction in fuel economy (1–2 mpg typical)
TPMS sensors from factory wheels may not transfer to new wheels — budget for new sensors if needed
33s are the practical maximum on a standard-travel lift; 35s require UCAs and 3"+ lift plus trimming

title: Wheel Selection for the Tacoma — 17" Steel, Alloy, and Beadlock

citations.title: Method Race Wheels 701 Trail Product Page
Tacoma World Wheel and Tire Fitment Thread

summary: The Tacoma's 6x139.7 bolt pattern is shared with 4Runner, Tundra, FJ Cruiser, and Land Cruiser — wheel selection is wide open, but backspacing is the critical dimension for lifted IFS Tacomas, and getting it wrong causes CV binding and premature bearing wear.
description:
Backspacing and offset are the two dimensions that determine where the wheel sits relative to the hub. For a lifted Tacoma with UCAs, the target backspacing is 4.75"–5" (approximately 0mm to +5mm offset in the 17x9 format). Too much backspacing pushes the wheel inward, where it contacts the inner fender and upper control arm at full compression. Too little backspacing pushes the wheel outward, which widens the track but can create tire-to-fender contact and increases stress on the wheel bearing.

Pro Comp steel wheels are the budget choice — at $89 each they're the most affordable way to mount a set of 33s, they're nearly indestructible, and they're easy to true or replace in the field. The tradeoff is weight: a 17x9 steel wheel runs about 28–32 lbs vs 18–22 lbs for a comparable alloy. On a Tacoma running trail, the weight isn't a performance issue, but it does increase rotating unsprung mass which dulls suspension response slightly.

Method Race Wheels 701 Trail is the most popular alloy choice in the Tacoma community for good reason — the spoke pattern resists mud packing, the finish is durable, the offset is correct for 2.5"+ lift, and they're Made in the USA. The 17x8.5 size pairs optimally with 285/75R16 (33") tires and the IFS geometry of the Tacoma. Fuel and Black Rhino offer comparable designs at lower prices, though with slightly more variable finish quality and a wider spoke pattern that can pack mud in deep clay.

Beadlock wheels mechanically clamp the tire bead to the wheel rim, preventing bead separation at very low tire pressures (under 10 PSI). They're the correct choice for rock crawling where you air down to 8–12 PSI. For trail and overland use at 18–25 PSI, standard wheels with a quality tire are sufficient. Note that DOT-legal beadlock wheels (Raceline Mamba, Method 409 Beadlock) can be driven on-road legally; purely race-spec beadlocks typically are not street legal. Confirm the DOT marking before using on public roads.
steps: Confirm current and planned lift height — this determines the correct backspacing range (4.75"–5" for 2.5"+ lift)
Verify new wheel fits Tacoma hub bore — 106.1mm is the Tacoma hub bore; most aftermarket wheels use 108mm with hub-centric rings included
Mount tires to new wheels at a tire shop; balance at this stage
Transfer TPMS sensors from old wheels to new — requires TPMS sensor removal tool and tire machine; confirm sensor compatibility
Install wheels on vehicle; torque lug nuts to 85 ft-lb in a star pattern
Check clearance at full compression and full lock before trail use
Recheck lug nut torque at 50 miles after install
